# Vigil — full text

> Vigil is a free, open-source softened geometric grotesk by Keno Vigil, under the SIL Open Font License 1.1. Eight weights with matching italics, an Outline style, and a continuous 200-900 variable axis. Free for commercial use: no cost, no account, no email, no attribution required. This file is the full text of vigilfont.com for machine readers.

Source: https://www.vigilfont.com/ · Install guide: https://www.vigilfont.com/install.md

---

# Install

Vigil is a free variable typeface under the SIL Open Font License 1.1. No account, no API key, no attribution required in your designs.

| | |
|---|---|
| CSS family name | `Vigil` |
| Weight axis | 200–900, continuous (`font-weight: 437` is valid) |
| Italic | Yes, on the same axis |
| Second family | `Vigil Outline` (weight 700, roman and italic) |
| Hosted stylesheet | `https://www.vigilfont.com/vigil.css` |
| CORS | `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on fonts and CSS, so hotlinking works from any domain |
| License | SIL Open Font License 1.1 (`OFL-1.1`) |

## 1. One line of HTML

The fastest path. No download, no build step.

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://www.vigilfont.com/vigil.css">
```

```css
body { font-family: "Vigil", sans-serif; }
```

## 2. Plain CSS

Paste this anywhere. It works hotlinked as written, or change the URLs to your own paths after downloading the two files.

```css
@font-face {
  font-family: "Vigil";
  src: url("https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/Vigil-wght-.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 200 900;
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;
}
@font-face {
  font-family: "Vigil";
  src: url("https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/Vigil-Italic-wght-.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 200 900;
  font-style: italic;
  font-display: swap;
}
```

Two files cover all eight weights and both slopes. You do not need the static files unless you are supporting browsers without variable font support.

## 3. Tailwind CSS

Tailwind v4, in your CSS entry point:

```css
@import "tailwindcss";
@import url("https://www.vigilfont.com/vigil.css");

@theme {
  --font-vigil: "Vigil", ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif;
}
```

Then use `font-vigil`. For Tailwind v3, in `tailwind.config.js`:

```js
export default {
  theme: {
    extend: {
      fontFamily: { vigil: ['Vigil', 'ui-sans-serif', 'system-ui', 'sans-serif'] },
    },
  },
}
```

## 4. Next.js

Self-hosted with `next/font/local`, which is the recommended path because it removes the network request and the layout shift. Download the two variable files into `app/fonts/` first.

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
import localFont from "next/font/local";

const vigil = localFont({
  src: [
    { path: "./fonts/Vigil-wght-.woff2", weight: "200 900", style: "normal" },
    { path: "./fonts/Vigil-Italic-wght-.woff2", weight: "200 900", style: "italic" },
  ],
  variable: "--font-vigil",
  display: "swap",
});

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en" className={vigil.variable}>
      <body style={{ fontFamily: "var(--font-vigil)" }}>{children}</body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

```bash
curl -O https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/Vigil-wght-.woff2
curl -O https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/Vigil-Italic-wght-.woff2
```

## 5. Vite, React, Svelte, or any bundler

Put the two woff2 files in your static or public directory, then paste the `@font-face` blocks from section 2 with local paths into your global stylesheet. Import that stylesheet once at your app entry point.

## 6. Desktop, for Figma, Sketch, Word or Illustrator

```
https://www.vigilfont.com/downloads/Vigil.zip
```

About 2.4 MB. Unzip it, select the `Vigil-*.ttf` files at the top level, and double-click to install. On Windows, extract the zip before installing; Windows will not install fonts from inside an archive. Figma and Sketch read your installed system fonts, so quit and reopen the desktop app afterwards. Figma in the browser needs their font installer running.

## Using the variable axis

The weight axis is continuous, so any integer between 200 and 900 is real.

```css
.lede { font-weight: 437; }
```

Named weights map as: ExtraLight 200, Light 300, Regular 400, Medium 500, SemiBold 600, Bold 700, ExtraBold 800, Black 900.

## Optional typographic features

```css
/* single-storey a */
.alt-a { font-feature-settings: "ss01" 1; }

/* tabular figures, for tables and timers */
.numbers { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
```

Vigil also carries fractions, superscripts and subscripts, and kerning throughout.

## Files

| Purpose | URL |
|---|---|
| Drop-in stylesheet | `https://www.vigilfont.com/vigil.css` |
| Variable roman | `https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/Vigil-wght-.woff2` |
| Variable italic | `https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/Vigil-Italic-wght-.woff2` |
| Outline roman | `https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/VigilOutline-Regular.woff2` |
| Outline italic | `https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/VigilOutline-Italic.woff2` |
| Full family zip | `https://www.vigilfont.com/downloads/Vigil.zip` |
| License text | `https://www.vigilfont.com/OFL.txt` |

Static WOFF2 for all sixteen roman and italic weights are at `https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/Vigil-{Weight}.woff2`, for example `Vigil-SemiBoldItalic.woff2`. TTF and OTF are inside the zip.

## Character set

Latin Extended: Western and Central European, covering English, Spanish, French, German, Polish, Czech and Turkish among others.

## Changes

**1.004 (2026-09-18).** The tail comes back off the lowercase `l`, and the capital `I` takes a short crossbar instead. The tail did separate `l` from `I`, but it fell on one of the most frequent letters in English and its curve reads as a mirrored `J` wherever nothing follows it. The `I` does the same job on a rarer letter, in a shape nothing else claims. Stylistic set 2 goes back to giving the *tailed* `l`, as it did at 1.000 and as Figtree ships it; the full-serif `I` stays on it, as it always has. `ł` and the accented forms follow. Nothing else changed.

**1.002 (2026-09-17, not released).** The tailed `l` is spaced properly. It shipped with no right sidebearing at all, so it crowded whatever followed, and from SemiBold up its tail crossed into the next letter. The bearing is now set tight, and kerning gives the space back only where the tail actually collides: before `.` `,` `:` `;` and before `x` and `z`. No letterform changed, and the italics were already correct.

**1.001 (2026-09-16).** The lowercase `l` now has a tail by default, so `l` and `I` read apart at every weight; the accented `ĺ ľ ļ` follow. Stylistic set 2 (`ss02`) is reversed: it now gives the *plain* `l`. If you had `ss02` on to get the tail, turn it off. `ł` follows, since Figtree draws a tailed one as well.

## Rounded by rule, not by default.

Kt

Most at the terminals.

Ez

Less at structural corners.

lL1

Even on the stems, small enough to keep the edge.

Vigil is a free variable typeface by Keno Vigil — a geometric grotesk with a large x-height, a double-story a and a single-story g. Rounding is applied by rule — most at exposed terminals (C G S c e s, the arms of E F T, the feet of K and z), then a smaller, even radius at structural corners and on the stems of l, L, 1 and I, which keep enough edge to stay apart. At 16px it reads as a clean sans. At 96px the softness becomes the signature.

Text, 16px
Type is the interface. A body face earns its place in the first paragraph, not the first headline. Vigil keeps its counters open and its spacing even at small sizes, so long passages stay quiet and the rounding never announces itself. Set it at 16 over 24 with a measure near sixty-five characters, and the page reads like it was never designed at all — which is the point.

## Questions, answered.

### Is Vigil free for commercial use?

Yes. Vigil is released under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, so you can use it in commercial work, embed it in apps and websites, and sell products set in it. There is no cost, no account, and no attribution required in your designs.

### What is Vigil based on?

Vigil is derived from Figtree, Erik Kennedy's open-source geometric sans, under the SIL Open Font License. Figtree supplies the skeleton. The rounding rules, the outline style and the finished curves are Vigil's own.

### How many weights does Vigil have?

Eight weights, from ExtraLight 200 to Black 900, each with a matching italic. There is also a separate Vigil Outline style in roman and italic. One variable font file covers the whole 200 to 900 axis.

### Can I use Vigil in a logo?

Yes. The SIL Open Font License places no restriction on what you set in the typeface, logos and wordmarks included. The one thing the license forbids is selling the font files on their own.

### Which languages does Vigil support?

Vigil covers Latin Extended, which includes Western and Central European languages such as English, Spanish, French, German, Polish, Czech and Turkish. Kerning runs throughout, alongside tabular figures, fractions, superscripts and subscripts.

### How do I self-host Vigil on a website?

Download the zip, copy the two variable WOFF2 files to your server, and add the two @font-face rules from the download section below. One file covers all eight weights. Static WOFF2 and TTF files are included for older browsers.

### Is there a matching icon set?

Yes. Vigil Icons is a companion set of 111 icons drawn on the same 24px grid as the type, and every one of them is free with no email — the same terms as the font. SVG, PNG, sticker packs and Slack and Discord emoji.

## Using it takes about a minute.

Three ways in, depending on what you are. Every snippet below is real and copyable — nothing here needs an account.

Designers

### Install it like any other font.

Download, unzip, select the 16 Vigil-*.ttf files sitting right there in the folder, double-click, Install. Nothing to dig through — they are at the top level on purpose. On Windows, extract the zip first; it will not install fonts from inside one. There is a Read me first.txt in there if anything goes sideways. Figma and Sketch read your installed fonts — quit and reopen Figma’s desktop app and Vigil appears in the picker. On Figma in the browser you need their font installer running.

Download the family — 2.4 MB ↓

Developers

### One line, no build step.

Served with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so it works from your domain without downloading anything.

HTMLCopy

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://www.vigilfont.com/vigil.css">

CSS — self-hosted, or paste as-isCopy

@font-face {
font-family: "Vigil";
src: url("https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/Vigil-wght-.woff2?v=1.004") format("woff2");
font-weight: 200 900;
font-display: swap;
}
@font-face {
font-family: "Vigil";
src: url("https://www.vigilfont.com/fonts/Vigil-Italic-wght-.woff2?v=1.004") format("woff2");
font-weight: 200 900;
font-style: italic;
font-display: swap;
}

One variable axis, so font-weight: 437 is a real value, not a rounding error.

Writers

### Slides, decks, documents.

Mac — unzip, select the TTFs, double-click, Install Font. Vigil is then in Keynote, Pages, Word and Canva’s desktop app. Windows — select the TTFs, right-click, Install.

Canva — Brand Kit → Brand Fonts → Upload. Note that font upload is a Canva Pro feature; the desktop app reads your installed fonts for free instead.

Google Docs cannot do it. Docs only loads fonts from Google’s own library, so no uploaded font works there — Vigil included. That is a Docs limitation, not a licensing one.

# Notes

## The airport font is Frutiger, mostly — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/airport-font

2026-09-21 — Keno Vigil

# The airport font is Frutiger — and Heathrow ran a serif

One typeface was drawn for an airport and ended up in hundreds of them. The airport that refused it spent a decade proving the received wisdom wrong.

ces

The airport font is Frutiger. Adrian Frutiger drew it for the new Paris airport at Roissy — Charles de Gaulle — and it was released commercially in 1976 by Stempel with Linotype, under its designer's name. It is not required anywhere. No standard names it. Airports simply keep choosing it, which is a better endorsement.

That is the short answer. The longer one: terminal signage is among the least regulated public typography there is, the runner-up is Helvetica, and the world's busiest international airport spent a decade running its signs in a serif, with test data behind it.

## A typeface commissioned by an airport

The brief came with a building attached. Paris was building an airport from nothing at Roissy and needed a directional sign system to open with. Terminal 1 — Paul Andreu's circular ten-storey drum ringed by satellites — was inaugurated on 8 March 1974 by prime minister Pierre Messmer. The first commercial flight landed five days later.

The obvious move was to set the signs in Univers. Frutiger had designed it, it was everywhere, and its systematic range of widths and weights was exactly what a sign programme wants. He turned it down.

His reasoning was about the reader's situation, not the letters. Univers was drawn for a page held still at arm's length. An airport reader is walking, dragging a bag, looking up at an angle, in a hurry, often not reading in their first language. The failure mode there is not that a letter looks wrong. It is that letters stop being distinguishable — the round ones collapse toward a common blob, and the word loses its silhouette.

So the new alphabet opened up. The apertures of c, e and s widened so the openings stay open at speed. The x-height rose relative to the caps, putting more of the word at the larger size. Similar characters were pulled apart. It was named Roissy.

c e s a — 1 l I
The letters that decide whether a sign works: the open ones, and the ones that turn into each other. Shown in Vigil, not in Frutiger.

The commercial family followed. Stempel, with Linotype, issued it in 1976 as Frutiger.

## The date nobody agrees on

Worth flagging, because this gets copied wrong forever: sources do not agree on when the commission arrived. Some say 1968. Some say 1970. Some say 1970–71, with the signage alphabet finished around 1972. That is a two- or three-year spread on the founding fact of the most-used signage typeface in the world, and the pages stating it most confidently are the ones with no source at all.

Not in dispute: the alphabet was drawn for Roissy, it was in place for the airport, and the retail family arrived in 1976 under a new name. Anyone giving you the exact month is guessing.

## Heathrow ran a serif, on purpose

Here is the part every listicle leaves out. Through most of the period when Frutiger was becoming the default, the British Airports Authority used a custom typeface called BAA Sign Bembo, designed for Heathrow around 1994 by Shelley Winter with Freda Sack. It is exactly what the name says: a serif, cut very bold, on a high x-height, and never commercially released. Frutiger replaced it only in the Heathrow rebuild of roughly 2006–09.

A serif, in the world's busiest international terminal, for a decade, against everything designers say about signage.

And when Heathrow chose a replacement, somebody actually tested it. Robert Waller's paper Comparing typefaces for airport signs, in Information Design Journal in 2007, combined legibility testing, consumer research and expert review to inform that decision.

The result was not the one the experts predicted. The serif performed as well as the sans in legibility testing. What mattered more than serif or sans was character width — and the condensed sans performed relatively poorly.

> The variable everyone argues about turned out not to be the variable. The one nobody mentions — how wide the letters are — turned out to be it.

It is the most useful finding in airport typography and almost never cited, because it is inconvenient. "Use a sans serif" is a rule people enjoy repeating. "Use something wide enough" is less satisfying and more correct.

## What is actually standardised — and what isn't

Aviation regulates almost everything, and largely not the letters on a terminal sign. Two things beside it are standardised, and the contrast is instructive:

- The pictograms. In 1974 the US Department of Transportation commissioned the American Institute of Graphic Arts, which worked with Roger Cook and Don Shanosky of Cook and Shanosky Associates. They surveyed the symbols already in use worldwide, rated them for legibility, international recognisability and resistance to vandalism, and drew 34 symbols, published that November as Symbol Signs. Sixteen more followed in 1979. They are copyright-free. The luggage, the escalator, the figures on the toilet doors: a 1974 federal design project.

- The airfield. Outside the terminal, signs are specified in detail. The FAA's advisory circulars AC 150/5340-18 and AC 150/5345-44 cover the siting, design and construction of runway and taxiway signs, down to five defined sign sizes with legend heights of 12, 15 and 18 inches for ordinary taxiway guidance.

So the suitcase symbol is standardised, and the letter a pilot reads at 30 knots is standardised, and the typeface a passenger reads on the way to gate B24 is whatever the operator liked. Less an oversight than an admission: the airfield sign has one reader doing one task. The terminal sign has forty million readers doing everything.

## The other answer is Helvetica

American terminals lean the other way. The Port Authority of New York & New Jersey commissioned Paul Mijksenaar in 1999 to build one signage system across JFK, Newark and LaGuardia, and what makes it work is not the typeface — it is the colour coding. Yellow for flight information: gates, ticketing, check-in. Green for ground transportation. Black for amenities. The later wayfinding manual, a 2021 SEGD Honor Award winner, describes the lettering as a restyled Helvetica.

Colour carries the category; type carries the name. A passenger scanning for a gate is filtering to the yellow signs and then reading. Get the filter right and the typeface has an easier job than designers assume.

One statistic to distrust while you are here: 75% of the world's airports use one of three typefaces — Helvetica, Frutiger or Clearview. It is quoted everywhere in the same words, and traces back to design trade-press pieces from 2014 and no further. No survey, no methodology, no sample. It may be roughly right. It is also exactly the shape of a number that gets repeated until it is true.

## Airports are leaving the shared alphabet

The recent movement is away from the off-the-shelf choice and toward commissioned type, for reasons that have nothing to do with legibility. Amsterdam Schiphol is the clearest case. Bureau Mijksenaar has worked on its wayfinding since 1990, and Frutiger was its signage face for decades. In 2025 the airport replaced it: a new identity by the studio thonik, with a custom sans serif built by the type foundry Bold Monday and called Royal Schiphol Group Variable. The stated objection was not that Frutiger failed. It was that it felt cold — clear and functional, and no warmer than that.

An honest reason, and a melancholy one. A typeface drawn to be invisible under stress was eventually found guilty of being invisible.

## What a type designer takes from this

Width is doing more than weight. The Heathrow research found character width mattered more than the serif question, and condensed sans serifs performed worst. Designers reach for a condensed cut whenever space is tight. But the scarce thing on a sign is not horizontal room, it is the reader's certainty about which letter they are looking at, and condensing spends exactly that. The same conclusion turns up in the road-sign research, where the narrowest FHWA series was eventually abandoned as illegible.

Rules about categories are usually rules about specimens. "Sans serif for signage" survives because nobody tests it. When Heathrow did, the serif held its own. That does not make serifs good for signage — it means the category was never the operative variable, and a rule stated at that level will be wrong at random.

The reader's body is part of the brief. Frutiger's design argument was about someone walking, carrying, glancing up, reading a second language. Not one of those is a typographic fact. All of them changed the letterforms. The equivalent question for interface type is not what size the text is; it is whether the person is sitting still.

And the Schiphol decision is where this stops being about legibility at all. Once a typeface clears the functional bar the argument moves to tone, and tone wins eventually. Not a failure of engineering — what happens when engineering succeeds and there is nothing left to fix.

## Can you download the airport font?

Not free, no. Frutiger is licensed through Linotype and now Monotype, and the files on free-font sites are unauthorised copies of a typeface somebody is still selling. BAA Sign Bembo was never released at all.

If you want the behaviour rather than the drawing, the useful category is the humanist sans serif: open apertures, generous width, a tall lowercase, characters kept apart. Under open licences that includes Fira Sans, Source Sans 3 and Public Sans. None is a Frutiger clone and none should be sold as one; what they share is the logic, which does the work.

Vigil is not a wayfinding typeface and a terminal is the wrong place for it. It is a geometric sans built for screens and paragraphs, and a geometric skeleton is precisely what the Roissy brief rejected — circles read as circles at distance, the failure Frutiger was drawn to avoid. What carries over is the part that generalises: a large lowercase, counters kept open rather than closed for style, and a 1, l and I you can tell apart. The counters are where legibility lives, at the gate and on the page alike.

## The baseball jersey font is not a font — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/baseball-jersey-font

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-21 — Keno Vigil

# The baseball jersey font isn’t a font

Thirty clubs, no shared alphabet, and a rulebook that legislates height and nothing else. The letters on an actual jersey were cut with a blade.

034

There is no baseball jersey font. Every club owns its own lettering, most of it drawn as artwork rather than built as a typeface, and none of it licensed to anyone. Major League Baseball's rulebook specifies that back numbers be at least six inches high. On what they should look like, it is silent.

That silence is the story. A hundred and thirty years of American lettering grew in the gap it left, and the shapes that filled it were decided less by designers than by the blade that cut the cloth.

## What the rulebook actually says

Rule 3.03 is short and almost entirely about conformity rather than form. All players on a team must wear uniforms identical in colour, trim and style, carrying numbers at least six inches high on the back.

Names get one sentence more. A league may provide that uniforms include player names on the back; if it does, every uniform on the team must have one, and any name other than the surname needs approval from the Commissioner's office. That last clause is why nickname jerseys are an event rather than a default.

Six inches. That is the entire typographic specification governing the most photographed lettering in American sport — against a British number plate, whose stroke width is written into law.

## How the numbers got there

Numbers were an experiment before they were a rule, and the experiment failed first. On 26 June 1916 the Cleveland club took the field at League Park with numbers on their left sleeves — the first major league team to try it. They were small, home-only, and dropped within weeks. Cleveland moved them to the right sleeve in 1917, then gave up.

The permanent version arrived in 1929. On 22 January the Yankees announced numbers on the backs of their uniforms, assigned by position in the batting order: Babe Ruth batted third and wore 3, Gehrig batted fourth and wore 4. Cleveland announced the same weeks later.

Then the weather intervened. The Yankees' 16 April opener was rained out, so Cleveland played in numbered uniforms first — the team that planned it lost the record to a cancelled game. By 1931 every American League club had numbers.

## Then Veeck put the names on

Player names are newer than most people assume, and they came from television. Watching the White Sox during the 1959 pennant race, Bill Veeck noticed that broadcast graphics put players' names on screen, and wondered why a fan at home should know something a fan in the ballpark didn't. In 1960 his White Sox became the first Major League team — and the first North American professional team in any sport — to wear names on the back.

He put them on the road uniforms only, reasoning that Chicago already knew its own players; home uniforms followed the next year. Not everyone was pleased. The second baseman Nellie Fox summed up the objection: we look like semi-pros.

Within months, all eight teams in the new American Football League were wearing names too.

## Four families, thirty drawings

The styles sort into four families. Every team's version inside a family is its own object.

- Old English. The oldest. Amateur-era clubs generally wore no lettering or a single letter, often blackletter. The National Baseball Hall of Fame's uniform history records the earliest known nickname display as the 1860 Excelsiors of Brooklyn — EXCELSIOR embossed in Old English on the team belt, not the shirt. The fad passed by the mid-1870s; it survives on a few caps.

- Block. The twentieth century's default, and an import from college athletics: Harvard's baseball team embroidered an H onto flannel jackets in 1865, and the letterman tradition that grew from it put one enormous chenille letter on a chest. Heavy, flat-sided, cut-friendly.

- Script. The earliest known script on a professional uniform is 1902, when Oakland and San Francisco of the California League put their city names across the front in it. The family that most obviously is not type.

- Tuscan. The one with flared, split or pointed stroke ends, borrowed wholesale from nineteenth-century wood type. It reads as "old-time baseball" now for the simple reason that it was the display idiom of the period.

## The blade drew the letters

Here is the part that explains the shapes, and it has nothing to do with taste. Jersey lettering is tackle twill. Letters and numbers are cut from layered polyester twill, heat-pressed together and onto the shirt, then sewn around every edge with a zig-zag stitch. It is the construction behind authentic baseball, football and hockey jerseys, and it is a manufacturing process pretending to be typography.

A blade and a sewing foot have opinions. Both want closed outlines and no hairlines — a thin stroke cut from cloth frays, and a tight inside corner is where a zig-zag stitch bunches. Both want counters big enough to stitch around, and long simple runs rather than fussy transitions.

3 8   0 6   4 1
The digits a numeral set lives or dies on, at the distance a jersey is actually read. Shown in Vigil, not in any team's numerals.

So the athletic-block alphabet — chunky, flat-sided, generous in the counters, no thin strokes anywhere — is not a style anyone chose. It is what survives being cut out of fabric and sewn onto a moving body. The same story as the stamping die behind licence plates: the tool drew the letters, and the look came afterwards.

## 2024, or what happens when you shrink them

Nike became MLB's on-field supplier in 2020 under a deal announced in January 2019, replacing Majestic, with Fanatics manufacturing. In 2024 the league moved all thirty clubs to a new Vapor Premier jersey, and the lettering changed with it.

Sizes were standardised: four inches on the front, eight on the back, names cut to two and a half. More consequentially, names and numbers stopped being multi-layer raised twill and became single-layer heat-pressed graphics.

The reaction was immediate and close to unanimous. Players complained to the union; fans called the jerseys cheap. The typographic charge was that the smaller, uniformly curved nameplate crowded long surnames and read as amateur — precisely Nellie Fox's complaint in 1960, arriving from the opposite direction. MLB and Nike announced larger lettering for 2025.

Note what the rulebook did during all this: nothing. Eight-inch back numbers clear the six-inch minimum comfortably. The part everyone objected to — the names — is the part no rule governs.

## The script nobody can credit

The Dodgers script is the most recognisable lettering in the sport, and its authorship is a blank. What is documented: Larry MacPhail took over the Brooklyn club in January 1938 and overhauled its look, and the uniforms unveiled that March carried the word Dodgers in script across the chest, underlined by a sweeping curve, in the blue that took the team's name. Who actually drew it is not recorded by any authoritative source. Font-download sites name a person with total confidence and cite nothing; the sports-design historians who have written about the 1938 change do not.

It also could not be a font if someone wanted it to be. The letters connect, the underline is drawn for that specific word at that specific length, and the whole thing is one object. Typing a different word in it would produce something that is not it — the same reason the Coca-Cola script is handwriting rather than a typeface.

## What a type designer takes from this

Manufacturing is a design collaborator whether you invite it or not. Nobody sat down to invent the athletic-block letterform; a blade and a zig-zag stitch narrowed the options until one shape was left. Any medium with a physical step — embroidery, vinyl cutting, engraving — does the same to your drawing. The useful question before starting is not what the letters should look like but what the production step will refuse.

Lettering is not type, and the difference is combinatorial. A wordmark is one object optimised for one word. A typeface has to produce every word, including the ones nobody thought of. That is why the Dodgers script cannot be a font and why the distinction still earns its keep: a designer who tries to turn a piece of lettering into a family has to rebuild it as a system, and most of what made the lettering good does not survive the translation.

Numerals deserve the attention letters get. A jersey is a numeral test at maximum difficulty — huge, moving, wet, seen from every angle including edge-on. The pairs to check never change: 3 against 8, 6 against 8, 0 against O, 1 against l and I. If a set of digits survives a torso at two hundred feet, it will survive a spreadsheet.

## Can you download a baseball jersey font?

Not the real ones, and the honest answer is more useful than a list. No MLB club licenses its numerals, and no team wordmark is available as a font. What is sold under those names is imitation — independently drawn approximations of wildly varying accuracy, from the same category of site that confidently names the Dodgers' draughtsman. A team name is also a trademark, which does not care what typeface you used to infringe it.

And for anyone actually making a jersey, the font question is the wrong one. Lettering shops do not set names in a font file; they cut them from twill using their own cut-file libraries. Ask a supplier for their block and script alphabets and you are asking for the thing that actually goes on the shirt.

Vigil is the wrong typeface for a jersey and it would be dishonest to pitch it as anything else. It is a geometric sans built for screens and paragraphs; a back number needs something far heavier and more condensed than its widest setting, drawn for a blade rather than a screen. What it shares with the good numerals here is the discipline: tabular figures that hold their column, open counters, and a 1, l and I you can tell apart. That test matters at reading distance too — just with less mud.

## The Coca-Cola logo isn’t a font — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/coca-cola-font

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-07 — Keno Vigil

# The Coca-Cola logo isn’t a font

It is a bookkeeper’s handwriting from 1886, in the penmanship style he already used at work. Nobody designed it. Somebody just wrote it down.

CC

There is no Coca-Cola font. The wordmark was written by hand in 1886 by Frank Mason Robinson — bookkeeper and partner to John S. Pemberton, who had invented the drink — as an adaptation of Spencerian script, the ordinary business penmanship of the day. It has been redrawn many times since. It has never been a typeface you could install.

That distinction sounds pedantic and isn't. It explains why the logo has outlived every typographic fashion of the last hundred and forty years.

## The bookkeeper named it, then wrote it

Robinson did two things that are still visible on a can today. First, he proposed the name — reasoning, in the company's own telling, that the two Cs would look well in advertising. That is a lettering judgement, not a marketing one. He picked the name partly because of how it would look written down.

Then he wrote it down. He experimented with an adaptation of Spencerian script, and what he produced was adopted by everyone at Pemberton's company by unanimous consent. The script began appearing in Atlanta newspaper advertising the following year.

Consider how little apparatus was involved. No brief, no studio, no rounds. A man who was good at handwriting because his job required good handwriting wrote two words the way he wrote everything, and got them slightly more beautiful than usual.

## Why a bookkeeper had this in his hands

Spencerian script was not an artistic flourish in 1886. It was the standard hand of American business — taught in commercial schools, expected in ledgers and correspondence, the thing clerks were drilled in. Oval forms, a steady rightward slant, and thick-and-thin strokes that come from pressure on a flexible steel nib rather than from the shape of the pen.

So Robinson was not reaching for a decorative style. He was writing in his professional hand, the way you or I would type in whatever the default is. The most valuable wordmark in the world is, in origin, a competent professional doing his ordinary job slightly better than he had to.

That is also why it looks the way it does. The swelling stems, the long lead-in stroke, the way the two Cs throw those descending tails underneath the word — none of that was drawn to be a logo. It is what a flexible nib does when a trained hand moves quickly.

## What the nib is doing

Look at any stroke in the wordmark and you will see it start thin, swell through the middle, and taper again. That is not a drawn outline. It is the physical behaviour of a pointed flexible nib: the tines spread under downward pressure and close when the pressure lifts, so weight follows force rather than direction.

This is worth separating from the other way scripts get their contrast. A broad-edge pen — the chisel-tipped kind used for blackletter and italic — produces thicks and thins from the angle of the nib against the direction of travel, with no change in pressure at all. Spencerian is the other family entirely, and it is why the strokes swell in the middle of a curve instead of on one particular diagonal.

Once you know that, the logo stops looking designed and starts looking performed. The long entry stroke before the C is a run-up, the way a runner needs a few steps before a jump. The tails under both Cs are exit strokes, the hand carrying on past the letter because stopping dead would be harder than continuing. Those are artefacts of movement, not decisions.

That is also the part imitations get wrong. A drawn approximation puts weight where a designer thinks it looks balanced. A written one puts weight where the hand happened to press.

## The hand that wrote it disappeared

Spencerian script did not fade because taste moved on. It was made obsolete by a machine.

Business penmanship existed because commerce ran on handwriting — every ledger, invoice and letter was produced by a person with a pen, so the ability to write quickly and legibly was a hireable skill worth years of drilling. The typewriter removed the reason for it. Within a generation the ornamental business hand went from professional necessity to hobby.

Which means the Coca-Cola wordmark is a fossil of a vanished workplace competence. Nobody today writes that way because their job demands it, in the way Robinson did. The most reproduced piece of lettering on earth records a skill that stopped being useful about a century ago.

## Lettering and type are different crafts

This is the part worth internalising, because it is not obvious and it comes up constantly.

A typeface is a system. Every character has to work beside every other character, in any order, in words nobody has written yet. That constraint is enormous, and it is why type design is slow.

Lettering has no such obligation. Robinson only ever had to make these two words work, in this order, forever. He could let the C swing out further than any systematic C could, because no other letter would ever have to live next to that swing.

Almost every wordmark you can picture from memory is lettering, not type, and this is why. The freedom to solve one arrangement perfectly beats the discipline of solving all arrangements adequately — when you only need one arrangement.

## Why nobody has been able to replace it

Coca-Cola has modernised nearly everything else. The script has survived largely intact through Art Deco, modernism, the Swiss grid, the corporate-identity boom, the flat-design purge, and every phase since.

Part of that is simple recognition value. But part is that the mark is not of a period, because it was never fashionable to begin with. Spencerian script in 1886 was not a style choice; it was infrastructure. Marks born from a fashion age with it. Marks born from an ordinary practice sometimes don't.

There is also a mechanical reason. Because it is lettering rather than a font, it has no sibling characters to become dated alongside. A logo set in a 1970s typeface carries the 1970s in every letter. This one carries only itself.

## The fonts pretending to be it

Search for a Coca-Cola font and you will find several free downloads that approximate the script. They are unofficial, they are usually rough where the original is most careful — the entry strokes and the tail of the second C — and they exist to let people fake the mark.

Which is the actual reason to avoid them: the wordmark is a registered trademark. The problem with using a lookalike for your own brand is legal, not aesthetic. Nobody at Coca-Cola cares what font is on your birthday invitation; they care a great deal about a beverage company whose logo resembles theirs.

If you want that feeling honestly, use a well-drawn Spencerian or English roundhand script and letter your own word. You will get something better anyway, because a script cut for general use is drawn to handle any word, and yours only has to handle one.

## What a type designer takes from this

The lesson I keep returning to is about where identity actually lives.

Robinson had no design training and no theory. What he had was a practised hand and a name chosen partly for how it would look written. The mark works because the constraint and the craft were sitting in the same person, and he did not overthink it.

Modern branding tends to invert this: pick a typeface, then commission a designer to make it feel bespoke. It produces competent wordmarks that could belong to any of four companies. The 1886 process — write the thing, in a hand you actually have, until it looks right — produced something that could not belong to anyone else.

Vigil is on the other side of that line, and deliberately so. It is a system built to set words I will never see, which means it can never do what Robinson's two words do. A typeface that tried to be as distinctive as a wordmark would be unusable as a typeface — that is the trade, and the fonts people love to hate are mostly the ones that took the distinctive side of it and got handed to everybody.

## What font is easiest to read? — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/easiest-font-to-read

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-06 — Keno Vigil

# What font is easiest to read?

The honest answer is not a font name. It is a set of conditions — and the research on the fonts sold as easier to read is not kind to them.

Il1

There isn't one. Legibility is a relationship between letters and a particular reader under particular conditions, and among competently drawn text faces the differences are small — small enough that they are routinely swamped by size, line length and spacing. A well-set page in Arial beats a badly set page in anything.

That is an unsatisfying answer to a question people ask sincerely, usually because they are trying to do right by someone. So here is the useful version: what actually moves the needle, what demonstrably doesn't, and a test you can run in ten seconds.

## The serif versus sans argument is mostly noise

You have heard that serifs guide the eye along the line, and that sans serifs are cleaner on screens. Both claims are repeated with total confidence and neither survives contact with the evidence. Studies comparing the two have been run for decades and have failed to produce a consistent winner on reading speed or comprehension.

What they do produce is a pattern worth noticing: whenever a study finds a difference, it is usually smaller than the difference you get from bumping the type up two points. The variable everyone argues about is not the variable doing the work.

Use a serif or a sans because of what the page should feel like. That is a real reason. Just don't tell yourself it is a legibility decision.

## The uncomfortable part: dyslexia fonts

OpenDyslexic was released in 2011 by Abbie Gonzalez, with weighted bottoms on the letters intended to stop them flipping or rotating for readers with dyslexia. It spread fast, into schools and e-readers and accessibility toolbars, on an idea that sounds obviously right.

The research has not backed it up.

- In 2013, Luz Rello and Ricardo Baeza-Yates used eye tracking with Spanish readers aged 11 to 50 who had dyslexia. OpenDyslexic did not significantly improve reading time, and did not shorten fixations.

- In 2016, Kuster and colleagues asked readers with dyslexia which face they preferred among Arial, Times New Roman and dyslexia-specific designs. They preferred Arial.

- In 2017, Wery and Diliberto tested children with dyslexia across Times New Roman, Arial and OpenDyslexic in Annals of Dyslexia, and found no consistent gain for the dyslexia-specific face.

- In 2023, Broadbent compared Arial and OpenDyslexic with dyslexic and non-dyslexic students. Of those who expressed a preference, most chose OpenDyslexic — largely on how it looked. Test scores showed no difference by font.

That last finding is the one to sit with. People liked it, and it did not help them. Preference and performance came apart, which is exactly the trap that makes design decisions feel obvious and be wrong.

None of this means the fonts are fraudulent or that people who prefer them are mistaken about their own comfort. It means the specific claim — that these letterforms measurably improve reading for dyslexic readers — has been tested repeatedly and has not held up. And the same body of work found something more actionable: plain, unadorned faces did better than decorative or italic ones. The win was in the absence of noise, not in the presence of a special trick.

## What actually moves the needle

In rough order of how much they matter:

- Size. Nothing else in this list comes close. Most text on the web is set smaller than it should be because designers evaluate it at arm's length on a good monitor while young.

- Line length. Somewhere around 45 to 75 characters. Too long and the eye loses the return; too short and it breaks the rhythm every few words.

- Line spacing. Near 1.5 for body text. Tight leading makes the eye pick up the wrong line on the way back.

- Contrast. Grey text on white looks refined in a mockup and fails a tired reader on a phone in daylight.

- Character distinction. The first genuinely typeface-level item, and the one people never check. More below.

- Which family you picked. Last. Genuinely last, among faces drawn for text.

## Three settings that cost you more than any font choice

If the typeface is the last thing on the list, these are near the top, and all three are decisions people make for reasons that have nothing to do with reading.

All caps. Capitals throw away word shape — the pattern of ascenders and descenders that lets a reader identify a word before resolving its letters. It is the same reason American freeway signs moved to mixed case in 1958 and British ones followed, a change made on legibility grounds after testing rather than taste. A heading in caps is a stylistic choice with a real cost; a paragraph in caps is just harder to read.

Italics for long passages. Italic is a change of voice, not a body style. Set more than a few sentences in it and reading slows measurably. This is one of the few places the dyslexia research is unambiguous and positive: plain upright faces outperformed decorative and italic ones, which is a finding about restraint rather than about any particular font.

Justified text without hyphenation. Justification without a hyphenation engine opens rivers of white space through the paragraph, and the eye follows them downward instead of along the line. Left-aligned ragged-right is almost always the safer setting on the web, where hyphenation support is still uneven.

## Why people ask this question

Almost nobody asks it idly. It usually arrives attached to a real obligation — a form that older patients have to fill in, a school handout, a set of instructions for people who will be tired and in a hurry. The question is a proxy for how do I not fail this reader.

Which is why the font-name answer is worse than unhelpful. It converts a solvable problem into a shopping decision, and it lets everyone stop before they have done the part that would have worked. A document set at 12px in a beautiful accessible typeface is still set at 12px.

If someone hands you that brief, the useful reply is a question back: how big, how wide, how far away, and who is reading it in what light? Every one of those has a bigger lever attached to it than the font menu does.

## The ten-second test

Set this string in the face you are considering, at the size you will actually use:

Il1 O0 rn m
Capital i, lowercase L, one. Capital o, zero. R-n against m. Shown in Vigil.

If the first three are the same shape, you have a face that will turn Illinois into a picket fence and make every password, licence key and serial number a guessing game. If the O and the zero are indistinguishable, the same applies to anything numeric. If rn closes up into something like an m, you will get modern read as modem at small sizes.

This is the check that actually separates faces, and it takes ten seconds. It is also the one place where the choice of typeface genuinely beats a setting decision — no amount of extra leading will rescue a font whose l and 1 are the same drawing.

## Where the real accessibility work is happening

Atkinson Hyperlegible, released by the Braille Institute in 2019 and named for its founder J. Robert Atkinson, is instructive precisely because it does not claim a trick. It was drawn for readers with low vision, and its method is to push confusable characters further apart — some letters exaggerated well beyond what you would draw in a normal text face, because recognition matters more than evenness. It won Fast Company's Innovation by Design award for graphic design that year.

Note what it optimises. Not flow, not weighting, not some theory about how the eye moves. Just: make sure this character cannot be mistaken for that one. That is the mechanism legibility research keeps returning to, and it is the same mechanism Germany's licence plate typeface arrived at from a completely different direction, trying to stop a forger with a roll of tape.

## What a type designer takes from this

Two things, and the first is humbling if you draw type for a living.

The typeface is not the lever. If someone asks which font to use for a document their whole team has to read, the honest answer is to set it bigger, give it a sane measure, loosen the leading, and stop worrying about the family. Recommending a font feels like helping. Fixing the setting is helping.

The second is where a typeface does earn its keep: the confusable pairs. That is a drawing decision, it cannot be fixed downstream, and it is the reason Vigil keeps the tail on its l, the flag on its 1, and open counters at text sizes — the whole point of rationing the rounding rather than softening every corner. A face that blurs those is not a stylistic preference. It is a face that will cost somebody a wrong digit at the wrong moment.

## Fonts like Futura: what actually comes close — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/fonts-like-futura

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-14 — Keno Vigil

# Fonts like Futura: what actually comes close

Three free ones worth using, a run of 1930s knockoffs nobody mentions, and the substitute almost every list recommends for the wrong reason.

aoA

The closest free alternative to Futura is Jost. Poppins and League Spartan are the other two worth your time, and all three are open source. The catch is that no substitute is neutral: each one trades away something specific, and knowing which thing matters more than any ranking.

Most "fonts like Futura" lists are assembled by people who have never compared the letterforms. The usual top recommendation is Century Gothic, which is not really a Futura substitute at all — for reasons that are genuinely interesting once you follow the paperwork.

## What makes Futura hard to replace

Futura was drawn by Paul Renner and released by the Bauer Type Foundry in 1927. Four features do most of the work:

- A single-storey a — a circle with a stem, no bowl-and-hook. This alone identifies the family across a room.

- A small x-height with long extenders. The lowercase is short and the ascenders and descenders run long, which gives Futura its airy, slightly aristocratic texture.

- A near-perfect circular o, and round letters built from that circle rather than from an oval.

- A pointed apex on the A, and a sharply triangular M and W.

Here is the trap. Those are precisely the features that modern geometric sans-serifs soften, because every one of them costs legibility at small sizes. Enlarging the lowercase makes text easier to read and makes it stop looking like Futura. You cannot have both.

a o A
The three letters to check first in any candidate. Shown in Vigil, which answers all three differently from Futura on purpose.

## The 1930s were full of Futura knockoffs

The substitution problem is not new. Futura sold extremely well, and competing typesetting systems could not use Bauer's metal. So they made their own.

- Airport — Baltotype, 1930s.

- Twentieth Century — drawn by Sol Hess at Lanston Monotype, worked on from roughly 1936 into the 1940s, made so Monotype's machines had a Futura equivalent.

- Spartan — issued in 1939 for Mergenthaler Linotype with identical foundry type from ATF, aimed directly at Bauer's Futura.

None of these were tributes. They were commercial equivalents, produced because a printer who owned a Linotype machine could not buy Bauer's Futura and needed something that would set the same job. The history of geometric sans-serifs is mostly a history of machine compatibility.

## Century Gothic is a copy of a copy

Which brings us to the recommendation you see everywhere, and the reason it is misleading.

Century Gothic was released by Monotype Imaging in 1990. It is a redrawn version of Monotype's own Twentieth Century — already a Futura copy — with the widths adjusted to match ITC Avant Garde Gothic, Herb Lubalin's 1970 display face. The commercial motive was straightforward: it let Microsoft ship something metrically interchangeable with Avant Garde without licensing Avant Garde.

> A copy of a copy, refitted to a third typeface's measurements. Recommending it as "basically Futura" skips two generations of the family tree.

The practical consequence is visible. Century Gothic's lowercase is much larger than Futura's and its proportions are wider, because it inherited Avant Garde's widths. Set the same paragraph in both and the colour on the page is nowhere near the same. If you need to stand in for Avant Garde, it is excellent. For Futura it is a poor likeness with a good reputation.

## The free ones worth using

Three open-source families do the job honestly, and they fail in different directions.

Jost, by Owen Earl at indestructible type, is the closest. It is licensed under the SIL Open Font License, ships as a variable font, and is drawn from the same 1920s German geometric tradition rather than traced from Futura's outlines — Earl describes it as blending that precise German geometry with the legibility of English humanist faces. It has a small quirk of history: it was originally called Renner, after Futura's designer, and was renamed to Jost over intellectual property concerns. Naming a Futura homage after Paul Renner turned out to be a legal problem rather than a compliment.

Poppins, published by Indian Type Foundry in 2014 and free on Google Fonts under the OFL, is the most widely deployed geometric sans on the web. Its monolinear strokes and circular bowls are Futura-adjacent, but the x-height is far larger and the a is single-storey in a different, rounder way. Its real distinction is that it covers Devanagari as well as Latin — an internationalist take on a genre that was aggressively European.

League Spartan, from The League of Moveable Type, descends from Matt Bailey's Spartan and through it from those same early American geometric sans-serifs. It ships as a single variable file spanning Thin to Black. It is heavier and more compact than Futura and works best where you want the geometry to feel blunt rather than elegant.

## The paid ones, briefly

If the budget exists, the honest advice is usually to license Futura itself — Neufville Digital publishes it as Futura ND, drawn from the Bauer originals. Nothing imitates a typeface as well as the typeface.

Beyond that, Avenir (Adrian Frutiger, 1988) is the standard recommendation for people who want geometric character with humanist warmth and better text performance. It is worth being clear that Avenir is not an imitation: Frutiger set out to temper the geometric idea with the proportions of a readable text face, which is why it survives at small sizes where Futura struggles. If your actual requirement is "Futura, but it has to work in an interface", Avenir is usually the honest answer.

And Avant Garde remains the right answer when what you actually liked was Avant Garde — which, given how often Century Gothic is the face people have really been looking at, is more often than they expect.

## How to audition a substitute in ten minutes

Rankings are worth less than a test you run yourself, and the test is quick.

- Set a real paragraph, at the real size. Not the alphabet, not a headline. Roughly a hundred words at whatever size the work actually uses. Most substitution mistakes are invisible above 40px.

- Compare the texture, not the letters. Squint until the words blur. If one block looks noticeably darker or looser than the other, the proportions differ and your line spacing and measure will need redoing.

- Check the ambiguous set. Type Il1 O0 rn m. Geometric faces are prone to a capital I with no distinguishing feature and an O identical to a zero. Futura has this problem too; some substitutes make it worse.

- Count the widths. Type the same sentence in both and measure the line. A substitute that runs 8% wider will break every layout you already built.

- Look at the numerals. They are where cheap families fall apart, and where Futura's own figures — old-style in some cuts, with a distinctive one — surprise people.

If a candidate survives all five, it will survive the project. If it fails the width test, it is not a substitute no matter how similar the letters look.

## What a type designer takes from this

The useful lesson is that "similar" is not one measurement. Two faces can share a skeleton and diverge completely in texture, because texture comes from proportion — x-height against cap height, counter size, sidebearings — and not from the shapes of individual letters.

This is why swapping a typeface for a lookalike so often goes wrong in a way nobody can name. The letters look right in a specimen and the page looks wrong, because the line spacing, measure and colour were tuned to proportions the substitute does not share. When you audition a replacement, do it in a paragraph at the real size, never in a headline of the alphabet.

The second lesson is about what a constraint buys. Futura's small lowercase is a liability on a phone and the source of its entire character. The 1930s copies kept the proportions because printers needed a true drop-in. Modern free alternatives mostly do not, because they were drawn for screens. That is a defensible choice — it is just not the same typeface, and lists that rank them as interchangeable are measuring the wrong thing.

## Where Vigil fits, honestly

Vigil is not a Futura alternative, and it would be easy money to pretend otherwise on a page like this.

It is a geometric sans, and it shares the circular logic. But it has a large lowercase and a double-storey a, which are the two things that most define the difference. Set Vigil next to Futura and nobody would confuse them.

What Vigil is good for is the job Futura is genuinely bad at: sustained reading at text sizes on a screen, where a small lowercase and wide default spacing actively hurt. The sensible pairing, if you love the look, is Futura in display and something with a bigger lowercase underneath it. That is how most of the brands you associate with Futura — Nike among them — actually set their body copy. Vigil is free under the SIL Open Font License and drawn for that second job.

## Fonts similar to Avenir — and what they miss — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/fonts-similar-to-avenir

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-14 — Keno Vigil

# Fonts similar to Avenir — and what they miss

Avenir is already an answer to a question. Substitute it badly and you undo the thing it was built to fix.

oat

Montserrat is the closest free alternative to Avenir, with Nunito Sans the better pick for interfaces and long text, and Mulish the most restrained of the three. All are free under the SIL Open Font License. But the useful part of this question is not the list — it is knowing which of Avenir's properties you cannot afford to lose.

Because almost every "fonts similar to Avenir" list makes the same mistake: it recycles the Futura list. And Avenir is not a Futura-style geometric sans, which is the entire point of it.

## Avenir was built to break the geometry

Adrian Frutiger designed Avenir in 1987; Linotype released it in 1988. The name is French for future, and the reference is not subtle — it is a direct nod to Futura and the circle-based sans-serifs of the 1920s.

But Frutiger did not draw another one of those. He took the geometric idea and then deliberately violated it in three specific places:

- The vertical strokes are slightly thicker than the horizontals. A true geometric sans is monolinear — every stroke the same weight. That looks clean and reads poorly, because the eye uses weight differences to tell letters apart.

- The o is not a perfect circle. It is very slightly narrowed. A perfect circle is wider than every other letter in the alphabet and pulls the rhythm apart.

- The ascenders are shortened. Futura's long extenders are beautiful and waste vertical space; Avenir's restraint is what lets it set tightly without collisions.

None of those are compromises in the pejorative sense. They are the design. Avenir is Futura's clarity with the readability problems engineered out, which is why it survives at 14px and Futura does not.

o a t
Where Avenir shows its hand: a narrowed o, a double-storey a, a t with a real hook. Shown in Vigil, which resolves all three the same way for the same reasons.

## So the wrong substitutes are the strict ones

This is why the advice to replace Avenir with Jost, or with any rigorously geometric free face, gets it backwards. Those are good typefaces and they are solving the opposite problem — they restore the 1920s purity that Frutiger spent a career arguing against.

> Swapping Avenir for a strict geometric sans re-introduces every legibility issue Avenir exists to fix. It will look similar in a logo and worse in a paragraph.

If what you liked about Avenir was the circles, you actually liked Futura, and you should go and use Futura. If what you liked was that it stayed calm and legible through a long block of text, you liked the corrections, and you need a substitute that makes the same ones.

## Why the question gets asked at all

Almost nobody goes looking for an Avenir substitute because they dislike Avenir. They go looking because of how type is sold.

Avenir is commercial, and commercial type is not licensed the way software usually is. A desktop licence covers a fixed number of workstations, so a team that grows has to re-buy. A webfont licence is typically metered on monthly page views, so a site that succeeds gets a larger invoice. An app licence is separate again, and so is anything embedded in a PDF sent outside the company.

For a studio billing a client, that is a line item. For a one-person project, a nonprofit, or anyone shipping something that might quietly get popular, it is an open-ended liability attached to a design decision made in week one. That is the actual reason these searches exist, and it is a completely rational reason.

It is also worth saying plainly: the foundries are not being greedy. Type takes years to draw and there is no other way to get paid for it. But an honest answer to "what looks like Avenir" has to acknowledge that most people asking have a budget of zero and need a face they will never have to re-license.

## The free ones worth using

Montserrat, by Julieta Ulanovsky, released in 2011 and later redrawn by Jacques Le Bailly, is the usual best answer. It was drawn from the painted signage of the Montserrat neighbourhood in Buenos Aires rather than from any Swiss model, which gives it a slightly warmer, sturdier personality than Avenir. It is a touch friendlier and a touch less neutral. In display sizes the swap is close to invisible.

Nunito Sans is the flat-terminal companion to Nunito, which Vernon Adams drew with rounded terminals for display use; Jacques Le Bailly extended the family and produced the non-rounded version. Nunito Sans is the one to reach for in interfaces and long text — open apertures, a generous but controlled lowercase, and subtle stroke modulation that does the same job Frutiger's does.

Mulish, also begun by Vernon Adams and released under the OFL, is the most minimal of the three. Its one conspicuous divergence is a single-storey a, which is exactly the feature Avenir does not have. If your text is short, that reads as a stylistic choice; across a page it changes the texture noticeably.

All three are on Google Fonts, so hosting and licensing are non-issues.

Set side by side, the ranking depends entirely on the job. In a headline, Montserrat wins — it has the presence and the closest overall colour. In a paragraph at 15px, Nunito Sans wins, because its aperture and spacing were tuned for screens and Montserrat's wider forms start to feel loose. Mulish is the safest choice when the type should disappear entirely, provided that single-storey a does not bother you.

One thing none of them reproduces: Avenir's particular evenness across the weight range. Frutiger's family was planned as a system from the start, so Light, Book, Medium and Heavy sit at genuinely even intervals. The free families grew more organically, and their middle weights tend to cluster. If your design depends on a clear step between two adjacent weights, check that specific pair before committing.

## The one nobody mentions: you may already own Avenir

Worth checking before hunting for a replacement at all. Avenir Next ships with macOS and iOS. Frutiger reworked the family with Linotype's Akira Kobayashi from 2004, expanding the weights and widths and improving the fitting for digital use, and that reworked family is bundled with the operating system.

That covers desktop and print work on a Mac outright. It does not cover webfont use — a bundled system font is not a web licence, and self-hosting it would be a licensing violation. But a great many people looking for an Avenir substitute for a document, a deck or a poster have it installed already.

## How to check a candidate in five minutes

- Set 100 words at the real size. Not the alphabet. Avenir's virtues are text virtues and do not show up in a headline.

- Look for stroke modulation. Zoom into the o. If the sides and the top are identical in weight, it is a strict geometric and will not behave like Avenir in text.

- Check the a. Avenir's is double-storey. A single-storey a is an immediate, unmistakable difference.

- Measure the line width. Same sentence, both faces. Montserrat runs wider than Avenir; if your layout is tight, that is the constraint that will bite first.

- Test the numerals. Especially if anything tabulates — prices, times, data.

## What a type designer takes from this

Avenir is the clearest case in modern type of a family whose defining features are its deviations. Describe it by its system and you get "geometric sans-serif", which is nearly useless. Describe it by where it departs from that system and you get the actual typeface.

That generalises. The thing that makes any family feel like itself is usually not the rule it follows but the handful of places it declines to. A substitute chosen on the rule will always disappoint, because the rule is the part every other typeface in the genre shares.

There is a second, more practical lesson, which is that readable and pure pull against each other and somebody has to lose. Frutiger made that trade explicitly, in public, with his name on it. A lot of type decisions are the same trade made accidentally.

## Where Vigil sits

Vigil makes the same corrections Avenir does, for the same reasons: a double-storey a, a lowercase large enough to survive small sizes, counters kept open rather than geometrically ideal. If you are looking for an Avenir substitute because you need geometric character that holds up in body text, that is the shelf Vigil is on.

It is not an Avenir clone and will not pass as one. Vigil is softer at the corners and its geometry is more overt; Frutiger's proportions are the product of decades of signage work and are more finely tuned than mine. On a project where Avenir is already approved and licensed, keep Avenir. Where the budget is zero and the job is paragraphs, Vigil is free under the SIL Open Font License and was drawn for exactly that.

## A century of circles: the geometric grotesk — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/geometric-grotesk-history

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-08-28 — Keno Vigil

# A century of circles: the geometric grotesk

OGa

Three German typefaces appeared within about a year of each other and defined a category that is still with us. Jakob Erbar's Erbar came first, in 1926. Paul Renner's Futura and Rudolf Koch's Kabel followed in 1927. All three drew letters from the compass and the ruler — circles for O, C and G, triangles for A and V, straight strokes everywhere else — in the spirit of the Bauhaus conviction that form should come from construction rather than from the pen.

Futura won. Its perfectly round O and pointed apexes became shorthand for modernity, and it travelled further than any of its contemporaries — eventually to the Moon, on the plaque Apollo 11 left behind in 1969. But the pure geometric sans has a well-known flaw: circles and straight lines don't set comfortably as text. The letters fight each other for space, and long passages feel mechanical.

The second generation fixed that by cheating, gracefully. Herb Lubalin and Tom Carnase's ITC Avant Garde Gothic in 1970 kept the geometry but pushed it toward display, with famously tight spacing and ligatures. Adrian Frutiger's Avenir in 1988 went the other way: he described it as a geometric sans drawn by a human hand, with an O that isn't quite a circle and strokes that thin where they join. Avenir is the ancestor of nearly every "humanist geometric" that followed.

The current wave — Gotham, Circular, Figtree and their many relatives — inherits Frutiger's compromise and adds large x-heights tuned for screens. Vigil sits inside this tradition and makes one more adjustment: it treats the corners as a variable, not a constant.

If you want the practical version of this — how to recognise a geometric sans on sight, and which ones are worth using — that's the field guide.

## Geometric sans serif fonts: a field guide — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/geometric-sans-serif-fonts

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-04 — Keno Vigil

# Geometric sans serif fonts: a field guide

How to spot one in four seconds, why the strict ones are hard to read, and which are actually worth using.

OAao

A geometric sans serif is a typeface built from the compass and the ruler instead of the pen. Its O is close to a true circle, its strokes hold a single uniform weight, and its A comes to a point. Everything else in the category follows from those three decisions — including its famous weakness, which is that a perfect circle is a bad letter.

This is the practical guide. If you want the hundred-year argument behind it, that's a separate note.

## The four tells

You can classify a sans serif in about four seconds if you know where to look. Set the word Oahu and check these in order.

### 1. Draw a square around the O

A geometric O fills that square almost exactly. A grotesque O — Helvetica, Arial, Univers — is a slightly narrowed oval, taller than it is wide. A humanist O is narrower still and often visibly tilted. The circle is the single loudest signal in the category, which is why the letter O is on the cover of roughly every specimen ever printed for one of these faces.

### 2. Look for thick and thin

Geometric sans faces are monolinear: the vertical of the H and the curve of the O are drawn at the same weight. Most other sans serifs quietly thin their strokes where two curves join, because the eye reads an untreated joint as a dark blot. A face that refuses to do this is telling you it cares about construction more than optics.

### 3. Check the apex of the A

Compass-and-ruler construction gives you a triangle, so the A comes to a genuine point and the M is a pair of them. Flatten that apex and you are almost always looking at a grotesque instead.

### 4. Then look at the lowercase a — this one splits the category

This is the tell most guides get wrong. A single-storey a — a circle with a stem, the way a child draws it — means a strict geometric: Futura, Century Gothic, ITC Avant Garde Gothic, Poppins. A double-storey a, with the little hood over the bowl, means a humanist geometric: Avenir, Gotham, Proxima Nova, Montserrat, Figtree.

Oahu OAao
Vigil Regular — circular o, monolinear strokes, pointed A, double-storey a

Both are geometric sans serifs. But that one letter tells you which half of the category you're in, and the two halves are good at completely different jobs.

## Why the strict ones are hard to read

Reading is pattern recognition, and it runs mostly on the top half of the lowercase. The eye distinguishes letters by their differences — the way an n is not quite an h, the way a c opens where an o closes. Pure geometry works against exactly that. When every round letter is generated from the same circle, b, d, p, q, o, c and e converge on a single shape, and the reader has to slow down and disambiguate.

The 1920s originals compounded this with small x-heights. Futura's lowercase is short relative to its capitals, which looks elegant in a headline and turns a paragraph into grey soup. Set a page in Futura at 16 pixels and you will feel it in your neck.

None of which makes them bad typefaces. It makes them display typefaces that were marketed as text typefaces, which is a different problem.

## How the second generation fixed it

Adrian Frutiger's Avenir, in 1988, is the hinge. He kept the geometric skeleton and then broke the rules where reading demanded it: the O isn't quite a circle, the strokes thin slightly at the joints, the x-height goes up, and the lowercase a gets its second storey back. He described it as a geometric sans drawn by a human hand.

Nearly everything since has followed that compromise and pushed the x-height further for screens. That's the lineage running through Gotham, Proxima Nova, Circular, Figtree and their many relatives — geometric enough to feel constructed and modern, humanist enough to survive a thousand-word article.

## The ones worth knowing

### The originals

- Futura — Paul Renner, 1927. The category's definition and still its best display face. Went to the Moon on the Apollo 11 plaque. Small x-height; use it big.

- Erbar — Jakob Erbar, 1926. Beat Futura to the idea by a year and lost the century to it.

- Kabel — Rudolf Koch, 1927. The strangest of the three, with a tilted e and an oddly high waist. Worth using precisely because it's odd.

- ITC Avant Garde Gothic — Herb Lubalin and Tom Carnase, 1970. Geometry pushed to display extremes, with a famous set of overlapping ligatures. Almost impossible to set well and unmistakable when you do.

- Century Gothic — Monotype, 1991. The one already installed on your machine. Enormously wide, which costs you line length.

### The workhorses

- Avenir — Adrian Frutiger, 1988. The humanist geometric that made the rest possible.

- Gotham — Tobias Frere-Jones, 2000. Drawn from New York architectural lettering rather than Bauhaus theory, which is why it reads as American rather than German.

- Proxima Nova — Mark Simonson, 2005. Geometric proportions with grotesque details; for a decade it was the default voice of the web.

- Circular — Laurenz Brunner, 2013. The one every startup rebranded into, and still very good.

### The free ones

All of these are open-licensed and free for commercial use, which matters more than it should — a typeface you cannot afford to renew is a typeface you will have to redesign around later.

- Poppins — Indian Type Foundry, 2014. Strict geometric, monolinear, single-storey a. Excellent for headlines, tiring for paragraphs.

- Montserrat — Julieta Ulanovsky, 2011. Drawn from painted signage in a Buenos Aires neighbourhood, which gives it a warmth the Bauhaus faces don't have.

- Jost* — a Futura-inspired open-source revival, and the closest you'll legally get to Futura for nothing.

- League Spartan — another Futura-lineage face, heavier and better suited to display.

- Josefin Sans — unmistakably 1920s, with a very small x-height. A display face; treat it as one.

- Figtree — Erik Kennedy. A humanist geometric with a large x-height, built for interfaces. Vigil is derived from it.

- Outfit — clean, contemporary, geometric, and unusually consistent across its weights.

## Which one to pick

- For a headline or a logo, take a strict geometric. Futura, Poppins, Josefin Sans, Jost. The uniformity that hurts reading is exactly what makes a wordmark look inevitable.

- For body copy, take a humanist geometric with a large x-height. Avenir, Proxima Nova, Figtree, Vigil. You want the constructed feel without the reading tax.

- For an interface, prioritise x-height and a distinguishable 1/l/I over purity of geometry. Test at 13 and 14 pixels, not at 48.

- For signage, go wider and heavier than feels right on screen, and check the counters — the enclosed spaces in a, e and o are the first thing to fill in at distance or in the rain.

## Where Vigil sits

Vigil is a humanist geometric in the Avenir lineage: circular bones, large x-height, double-storey a, built to be set at sixteen pixels. Its one departure from the category is that it treats corner softness as a variable rather than a constant — rounded most at the exposed terminals where a stroke ends in open space, less at the structural joints, and not at all on the punctuation. The effect is that it reads as a clean geometric sans in a paragraph and only looks visibly rounded when you set it large. The reasoning is here.

It is not the best geometric sans on this page. Futura is a better display face and Avenir is a better book face. It is a good one that costs nothing and always will, which for a lot of projects is the specification that actually matters.
