## Highway Gothic vs Clearview: the fight over American road sign fonts — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/highway-gothic-vs-clearview

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-04 — Keno Vigil

# Highway Gothic vs Clearview: two fonts went to war over American road signs

The government approved the challenger in 2004, killed it in 2016, and brought it back in 2018 while refusing to endorse it. A story about halation, aging eyes, and twenty percent.

aes

The font on American road signs is called Highway Gothic. Formally it is the FHWA Standard Alphabets, drawn by Theodore W. Forbes and published in 1948, and you have read more of it than of any book you own. It is also the subject of the only typeface dispute in history to be settled, unsettled, and then re-settled by an act of the United States Congress.

## A wartime alphabet

The FHWA series came out of the Public Roads Administration during the Second World War, and arrived as six widths rather than one design: Series A through F, narrow to wide. The width you use depends on how much room the sign has. Series A is so condensed it was eventually abandoned as illegible; Series F is the generous one you get when the sign is big enough not to argue.

Then California changed it. Between 1949 and 1950, Caltrans engineers working on freeway signing took Series E and thickened its strokes to twenty percent of the letter height. The result — Series E-Modified — is the one you actually picture when you picture a road sign: wide, chunky, white on green.

The reason for the thickening is a detail almost nobody knows. Early guide signs weren't printed in reflective material. They were studded with button copy: dozens of small glass reflectors embedded along the spine of every letter, so headlights would light up the letterform as a constellation of dots. A stroke too thin couldn't hold enough buttons. The most recognisable letterform in American public life owes its proportions to the width of a piece of hardware.

The other decision that shaped modern signs came in 1958, when the AASHTO manual for Interstate signing made mixed case the standard for freeway place names. ALL CAPS had been normal. Mixed case won because word shape — the ascenders and descenders that give Baltimore a silhouette BALTIMORE doesn't have — is something the eye can catch at distance and at speed.

## Then the signs got too bright

Highway Gothic was drawn for a world of dim reflectors. Retroreflective sheeting kept improving through the following decades, and eventually it improved past the typeface.

The problem has a name: halation, also called irradiation or overglow. When a letter is bright enough, it appears to bleed outward. The glow spills into the enclosed spaces — the counters — of the letters that depend on them. A lowercase e fills in and becomes a luminous blob. An a stops being an a. And because Series E-Modified had those deliberately thick strokes, it had comparatively little counter space to lose.

This lands hardest on older drivers, whose contrast sensitivity declines with age, and on anyone driving tired in rain. It was, in other words, a public safety problem produced by an improvement.

## The challenger

Clearview was the answer. It was developed by Don Meeker and Christopher O'Hara of Meeker & Associates with James Montalbano of Terminal Design, working alongside Martin Pietrucha and Philip Garvey at the Pennsylvania Transportation Institute, with supporting research from Gene Hawkins and Paul Carlson.

The design strategy followed directly from the diagnosis. If halation eats counters, give it more counter to eat. Clearview opened up the problem letters — a, e and s — and raised the height of the lowercase relative to the capitals, so the letters carrying the word's shape are simply bigger. Committed to mixed case throughout. The claim from the research was roughly a twenty percent improvement in legibility and recognition at the same sign size, which in highway terms is enormous: it means reading your exit meaningfully earlier at seventy miles an hour.

aes — Baltimore
The three letters Clearview opened up, and why mixed case beat ALL CAPS. Shown here in Vigil, not in either highway face.

On 2 September 2004, the FHWA granted Clearview Interim Approval IA-5. Note the wording, because everything later turns on it: positive contrast, guide signs. Light letters on a dark background — white on green, blue, brown. Nothing else was approved. Not black-on-white speed limit signs. Not yellow warning signs.

## What went wrong

Two things, and neither is really the typeface's fault.

The first is that an interim approval covering one narrow case met a country of state highway departments who liked the new letters. Clearview started appearing where it had never been approved — in negative contrast, on regulatory and warning signs — and in the narrower widths. Subsequent evaluation found that in exactly those uses it performed worse than the Highway Gothic series it replaced. Dark letters on a bright ground have the opposite problem to halation: the background blooms inward and eats the letter, and generous open counters stop helping.

The second is subtler and more uncomfortable. When you replace an old sign with a new one, you don't only change the typeface — you change the sheeting, the sign, and often the size. Some portion of the measured gain was very plausibly the new sign, not the new letters.

On 25 January 2016, the FHWA terminated the interim approval. Existing signs could stay; new ones would go back to Highway Gothic.

## And then Congress got involved

The termination did not hold. States that had re-signed entire networks in Clearview now faced re-signing them again. Congress required the FHWA to review the prior research along with the safety and cost implications of its own decision, and on 28 March 2018 the agency reinstated the interim approval on the terms that existed before 2016.

It did so while stating that it made no recommendation or endorsement of the font.

> Approved, terminated, reinstated, unendorsed. Fourteen years, and the official position is that you may use it and they would rather not say.

So both typefaces are on the road today. Highway Gothic is the standard and the default. Clearview is permitted, on some signs, in some contrasts, at the discretion of the state. The next sign you pass is a vote in an argument nobody officially won.

## What about street name signs?

Different problem, same alphabet. The green blades on residential corners generally use the same FHWA series in a narrower width, because a street name has to fit a sign a fraction the size of a freeway gantry. This is where Series C and D earn their keep, and where you occasionally find a city that has commissioned something of its own and is quietly pleased about it.

The MUTCD requirement people notice most is the mixed-case one: street name signs moved away from ALL CAPS for the same reason freeway signs did in 1958. Word shape is information, and capitals throw it away.

## What a type designer takes from this

The lesson of the Clearview affair is not that Clearview was bad. It is a careful, well-researched typeface built by serious people to solve a real problem, and in the case it was designed for it appears to do so.

The lesson is that legibility is a property of a system, not of a font. The same letterforms that win in white-on-green lose in black-on-white. The same design that helps at a hundred feet of glowing sheeting does nothing on a printed page. Change the contrast, the size, the material or the distance, and the ranking changes with it. A typeface is not legible; a typeface is legible at something, for someone, on something.

Which is the argument for testing type in the conditions it will actually live in, rather than in a specimen. A face chosen because it looked convincing at 200 pixels on a designer's monitor is a face chosen under laboratory conditions that no reader will ever reproduce.

It is also, if I'm honest, the reason I started drawing letters at all. I grew up reading highway signs, and the thing that stuck was that letters which have to work outdoors, at speed, for strangers are the honest ones. Nothing on a road sign is there to be admired. Every decision in it is load-bearing.

## A footnote from Britain

Britain ran the same experiment and got a cleaner result. In the late 1950s and early 1960s, Jock Kinneir and Margaret Calvert designed the Transport typeface for British road signs, arriving independently at mixed case and at generous, open letterforms — and paired it with a matched system of pictograms and colour rules rather than treating the letters as a separate problem.

It was adopted, and it stayed adopted. Sixty years on it is still there, essentially unrevised. Designing the whole system at once, it turns out, is more durable than swapping the typeface inside a system built for a different one.

## Can you download either of them?

Not straightforwardly. The FHWA Standard Alphabets exist as federal engineering drawings rather than as a font you install, and the digital versions floating around vary a great deal in quality and fidelity. Clearview is a commercial typeface and is licensed as one.

If you want the highway idiom under an open license, Overpass — drawn by Delve Fonts and available through Google Fonts — is an interpretation of the Highway Gothic letterforms and is free to use.

Vigil is not a highway typeface and I am not going to pretend otherwise. It is a geometric sans built for text, with the same large lowercase and open counters that the road-sign research keeps arriving at, for the same underlying reason: the counters are where legibility lives.

## License plate fonts: shaped by a die, aimed at a forger — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/license-plate-fonts

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-04 — Keno Vigil

# License plate fonts: shaped by a die, aimed at a forger

Every other typeface is drawn for a reader. This one is drawn for a stamping die, a camera, and someone with a roll of black tape.

FE

There is no such thing as the license plate font. Road signs in the United States run on a single federal standard. Plates don't: every issuing jurisdiction picks its own, so North America alone carries dozens of variants, and a plate from Ontario and a plate from California are not speaking the same alphabet.

What they share isn't a design. It's a set of adversaries. A plate typeface has to survive a stamping die, resist a criminal with tape, and satisfy a camera — and only incidentally be read by a person. No other letterforms in daily life are designed under those conditions.

## The die drew the letters

Start with manufacturing, because manufacturing came first. A traditional plate is not printed. It is embossed: a die presses the characters up out of a flat sheet of aluminium, and the raised faces are then inked or foiled.

A die has opinions. It wants shapes it can cut accurately and press repeatedly without tearing the metal or wearing the tool. In practice that meant letters built only from straight lines and circular arcs — geometry you can lay out with a ruler and compass, and later specify exactly in CAD. It also meant a single uniform stroke weight, since a stroke that thins and thickens is a stroke that deforms unevenly under pressure.

That is the entire explanation for why plate letters look the way they look. The flat, industrial, slightly stiff quality isn't a style decision anybody made. It is what you get when the tool is a press rather than a pen.

The typographer Leeward Pro's survey of North American plate fonts — still the most thorough catalogue of these letterforms anywhere — sorts them into four construction types, and once you know them you cannot stop seeing them in traffic:

- Semicircular — straight sides closed off by half-circles top and bottom. Close cousins of Germany's DIN 1451, usually narrower.

- Squarish — bowls become boxes with rounded corners, typically true 90-degree arcs. Eurostile's industrial relatives.

- Oval — elliptical bowls and arcs, the closest these ever get to a humanist sans, though the mechanical construction and even stroke weight keep them firmly in the family.

- Hybrid — inconsistent, often with one logic for the letters and another for the numerals. Squarish alphas, oval digits.

## Germany drew letters against a criminal

The most interesting plate typeface in the world exists because the old one could be edited with tape.

West Germany used DIN 1451, an excellent engineering sans with a serious flaw in this specific job: its letters are too closely related to one another. A strip of black tape or a dab of paint turns a P into an R. An F or an L becomes an E. Against a backdrop of 1970s terrorism and ordinary plate theft, a registration you could edit by hand at the roadside was a genuine security problem.

The answer was FE-Schrift — fälschungserschwerende Schrift, "forgery-impeding typeface" — designed by Karlgeorg Hoefer between 1978 and 1980, introduced in 1994 and mandatory on German plates from November 2000.

F E   P R   3 8
The pairs a forger works on. FE-Schrift's job is to keep each one from becoming the other. Shown in Vigil, not FE-Schrift.

Its method inverts everything a type designer is normally taught. A good text family is built on shared parts — the same bowl in the b, d, p and q, the same shoulder in the n and m — because consistency is what makes a page feel like one voice. FE-Schrift refuses that. The letters are deliberately disproportionate, and no character is derived from any other. Each one is its own irregular object, precisely so that no amount of added ink turns it into its neighbour.

It is a typeface designed to be internally inconsistent on purpose, which is close to heresy, and it works. Several other countries adopted it, and the Mercosur bloc — Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay — standardised on it too.

## Britain legislated the stroke width

The British approach was to leave the drawing alone and regulate everything around it.

The typeface is Charles Wright, originally from 1935. The version in force is Charles Wright 2001, adopted by the DVLA as the single legal standard and modified for automatic number plate recognition cameras. Since 2001 it has been mandatory: no substitutions, no clever spacing, with only a 3D-effect variant permitted.

And the regulations are specific in a way typographers rarely see. Characters must be 79mm tall and 50mm wide — the 1 and the I excepted, for obvious reasons — with a stroke width of 14mm.

> A stroke width written into law. Most typefaces are lucky to get an opinion; this one got a statute.

The point of fixing the dimensions and the spacing is the same as the point of FE-Schrift's irregularity. If the gaps are legally defined, you cannot shuffle characters to make BD51 SMR read as a name, and a camera always knows where to look.

## Then the reader stopped being human

The quiet turn in this story is that the primary audience changed.

For most of the twentieth century a plate was read by a police officer, at distance, in bad light. Now it is read overwhelmingly by machines: ANPR and ALPR cameras at toll gantries, car parks and junctions, running at speed on infrared. Charles Wright 2001 was explicitly adjusted for those cameras. FE-Schrift's separation of similar characters serves them just as well as it serves against tape, because the failure mode of an algorithm and the failure mode of a forger turn out to be the same one: this character resembles that character too closely.

It is a rare case of security and legibility pulling in the same direction. Usually they don't.

## The die is gone. The shapes stayed.

Here is the part I find genuinely funny.

Embossing is on the way out. Flat plates, digitally printed on reflective sheeting, are cheaper, lighter and let a jurisdiction put whatever it likes on the background. Every manufacturing constraint that produced those stiff arcs and uniform strokes has evaporated. A flat plate could be set in anything.

And what do the states printing flat plates use? Digital replicas of the embossed fonts. The exact letterforms that a stamping die demanded, now reproduced by a printer that has never met a stamping die.

The constraint became the identity. Those shapes stopped meaning "this is what metal-forming permits" and started meaning "this is a licence plate" — and once a form carries meaning, the engineering reason for it is no longer load-bearing. This is skeuomorphism, but in aluminium, and nobody planned it.

## What a type designer takes from this

Two things, and the first is the same lesson the road-sign fight teaches from the other end.

Legibility is not a property a typeface has. It is a relationship between letters and a specific reader under specific conditions — and here the "reader" is a die, a camera, an officer and a criminal at once, wanting contradictory things. FE-Schrift is superb at its job and would make an atrocious book face. That is not a criticism of it. It is the whole idea.

The second is about distinctiveness, and it is more useful than it first appears. A text face gets its evenness from shared parts, and I build that way too — the same curve logic runs through Vigil's b, d, p and q. But the plate designers found the limit of that principle. When it matters most that this letter is not that letter, similarity becomes the enemy, and you have to give each character something no other character has.

Which is why the useful question when you are choosing type for anything that must not be misread — a dosage, a serial number, a code someone will type back — is not "is this legible?" It is "how far apart are the letters that could be confused?" Check the 1, the l and the I. Check the 0 and the O. Check the 8 against the B. A face that keeps those apart is doing the work a licence plate does, and a face that doesn't will fail in exactly the place it costs you.

## Can you download a license plate font?

Not the official ones, mostly, and it's worth knowing what you're actually getting. FE-Schrift and Charles Wright 2001 are regulated standards attached to legal specifications, not consumer downloads. Plate manufacture is a licensed business in most jurisdictions for good reason.

What circulate freely are replicas — independently drawn digital fonts based on observed plates, of varying fidelity:

- Penitentiary Gothic — often mistaken for a historical typeface, it's a 2003 commercial font by Andrew Leman and Richard Lucas, drawn from California plates specifically to make props for film and television. Its extra styles stack in different colours to fake the embossed relief.

- Driver Gothic — based on Ontario's letterforms.

- License Plate — Dave Hansen's, drawn from Washington state.

- Keystone State and Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania-derived.

Use them for what they are: period props, film work, and the pleasure of the reference. Do not use one to make a plate.

Vigil is not a plate font and would be a bad one — it is a geometric sans built for paragraphs, and it shares parts across letters on purpose, which is precisely the thing FE-Schrift refuses to do. What it does take from this corner of the world is the discipline underneath it: open counters, a large lowercase, and a 1, l and I you can tell apart. The counters are where legibility lives, whoever is doing the reading.

## The New York subway font isn’t the one you think — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/new-york-subway-font

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-08 — Keno Vigil

# The New York subway font isn’t the one you think

The signs are Helvetica. The famous manual wasn’t. Two typefaces have been quietly sharing the system for fifty years, and you can tell them apart from the platform.

es

The New York City subway is set in Helvetica — officially, and only since December 1989. The typeface in the famous 1970 sign manual, the one on the tote bags and the design-school reading lists, was a different face altogether: Standard Medium, an American rebadging of a German typeface from the 1890s.

This is the rare piece of design trivia where the popular answer and the correct answer are both true, just not at the same time. Ask what font the subway uses today and Helvetica is right. Ask what font Massimo Vignelli specified and Helvetica is wrong, by about nineteen years.

## The manual everyone cites specified something else

The document in question is the New York City Transit Authority Graphics Standards Manual, credited by the Museum of Modern Art to Massimo Vignelli, Bob Noorda and Unimark International, and dated 1966–70. That range matters. The manual is usually called a 1970 document, but the work behind it ran for four years before the binder existed.

What the manual specified was Standard Medium. Not Helvetica — which by 1966 was already the fashionable choice among modernists, and which Vignelli personally admired.

So the single most photographed piece of American wayfinding design is routinely credited to a typeface it does not contain.

## Standard was Akzidenz-Grotesk with an American passport

Standard was not an original design. It was Akzidenz-Grotesk, the German sans that Berthold made famous, sold under a different name for the English-speaking market. The renaming happened in the 1950s, when Amsterdam Continental began selling the typeface in New York and gave it a name a US printer would actually say out loud.

Its origins are murkier than the tidy version suggests. Research by Klim Type Foundry and the type historian Dan Reynolds traces the oldest weights to 1896, with the first weight published jointly by Bauer & Co. in Stuttgart and Berthold in Berlin in 1898 — and not under the Akzidenz-Grotesk name at all. They started life as Enge Steinschrift and Halbfette Bücher-Grotesk, and were gathered under one family name later.

Which means the typeface that ran New York for two decades was a nineteenth-century jobbing sans, assembled retroactively into a family, renamed for export, and then credited to the wrong typeface entirely. Type history is rarely as clean as the posters make it look.

## Why not Helvetica? Nobody is completely sure

The most honest source on this is also the most thorough one. Paul Shaw, a design historian, spent years on the question and published the results as Helvetica and the New York City Subway System in 2011. The subtitle is The True (Maybe) Story, and the parenthesis is not a joke — Shaw has said the hedge is there because he was not certain he had solved why Unimark and the Transit Authority landed on Standard rather than Helvetica.

The best-supported explanation is dull in the most instructive way: the signs were fabricated in the Transit Authority's own shop on Bergen Street, and that shop already held Standard. Adopting Helvetica would have meant buying and shipping large quantities of metal type from Europe. The budget decided the typeface.

> The most influential wayfinding system in America was set in whatever the sign shop already owned.

A second story circulates among transit-design people and is worth repeating with its label on: that Standard's J was not hooked enough for a system that runs an entire J line, and that Helvetica's more definite J helped push the switch. It is a good story. It is also the kind of detail that gets sharper each time it is retold, so treat it as folklore unless someone produces the memo.

What is documented is the shape of the transition. Helvetica did not arrive in a single changeover. It seeped in through the 1970s and 1980s as individual signs were replaced, until December 1989, when the Transit Authority made official a decision the maintenance schedule had already made for it.

## Bob Noorda did the part nobody photographs

Vignelli gets the name recognition. Noorda did the fieldwork, and the fieldwork is the actual design.

Before drawing anything, Noorda spent weeks riding the system and watching where people got lost, tracking the paths commuters took in order to find the exact points at which a rider needs to make a decision. He tested sign legibility in perspective — the way a sign is really seen, at an angle, from down the platform — rather than flat on a desk.

That produced the principle the whole system rests on: give the rider the information at the point of decision. Never before, never after.

It is worth noticing that none of that is typographic. The famous part of this project is a research finding about human behaviour in tunnels, and the typeface was the cheapest available vehicle for it. The fight over American road signs ran the same way — the argument that mattered was about legibility conditions, not letterforms.

## How to date a subway sign from the platform

Both typefaces are still down there, because the system has never been fully repainted at once. Telling them apart takes one glance at a lowercase s.

c e s
The three letters that give it away. Angled cuts mean Standard; flat ones mean Helvetica. Shown in Vigil, which is neither.

In Akzidenz-Grotesk, and therefore in Standard, the terminals — the cut ends of the strokes in c, e and s — are sliced at an angle. In Helvetica those same cuts are always horizontal or vertical. Helvetica's rigour is exactly this: every stroke ends square to the baseline, no exceptions, which is what gives it its slightly airless perfection.

Once you know it, older signage in the system stops being generic and starts being dated. Add the mosaic name tablets in the oldest stations — ceramic lettering that predates any of this and was never a font in the first place — and a single platform can hold three distinct eras of American public lettering.

## The map is a separate argument

Vignelli's other subway artefact is more famous and more contested: the 1972 diagrammatic map, built on 45- and 90-degree angles, with the geography of the boroughs bent to serve the diagram. Central Park became a small rectangle. Riders complained. It was replaced in 1979 by a more geographic design.

MoMA credits that map to Vignelli, Joan Charysyn, Bob Noorda and Unimark, and Charysyn's name is the one most often dropped in the retelling. Worth putting back in.

The manual itself has had a better afterlife than the map. Jesse Reed and Hamish Smyth crowdfunded a facsimile reissue in 2014, which found tens of thousands of buyers — a corporate sign specification turned collector's object, which is its own comment on how design remembers things.

## What a type designer takes from this

The uncomfortable lesson is that availability beat aesthetics, and the result was fine. The most admired signage system in the United States ran for two decades on a typeface chosen because it was already in the building. Nobody rode past their stop because of it.

The second lesson is sharper, and it cuts against Helvetica's reputation. Helvetica is not an obviously good signage face. Its apertures are tight — the gap in the c, the opening of the e — and tight apertures are the first thing to close up at distance, in glare, or in the blur of a moving train. Faces designed specifically for wayfinding tend to open those gaps deliberately. Helvetica did not win the subway on a legibility test. It won on supply, momentum and taste, and then became so associated with the system that changing it would now read as vandalism.

That is how signage typefaces actually get chosen. Not the best letterforms. The ones that were available, then defended.

## What you can actually use

Neither of these is free. Helvetica is licensed through Monotype, which also acquired Berthold's library and with it Akzidenz-Grotesk. There is no official free subway release, and the fonts marketed as one are unaffiliated redraws of varying quality.

If the goal is the look, the honest advice is to license the real thing or pick a neo-grotesque built for screens rather than a knock-off of a metal face.

And if the goal is Vigil: this is not the job for it. Vigil is a geometric sans, built on circles and straight lines, and the subway's whole aesthetic is grotesque — closed, neutral, deliberately unremarkable. Set a station name in Vigil and it will look like a brand, not a system. Where Vigil earns its place is the paragraph underneath the sign: the service change notice nobody can read, the timetable, the app. Open counters and a large lowercase do more work there than any amount of Swiss neutrality.

- 2026-09-06What font is easiest to read?The honest answer is that it depends on the reader, the size and the light — but the research narrows it a lot.

A geometric sans with open counters, a large lowercase, and a 1, l and I you can tell apart. Eight weights with matching italics, an outline style, and one variable file across the whole 200–900 axis. SIL Open Font License — no email, no account.

## The NFL font is three different answers — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/nfl-font

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-19 — Keno Vigil

# The NFL font is three different answers

The shield, the brand typeface and the numbers on the back of a jersey are three separate design problems. Only one of them has a name you can look up.

88

There is no single NFL font. The league's brand typeface is Endzone, a bespoke family drawn for the NFL by the foundry Village. NFL Network runs on a different face called Tackle. The numbers on a jersey are neither — those belong to the clubs and to Nike. Three questions wearing one search term.

Which one is being asked matters, because only one of the three has a name, and none of the three is available to download. Sorting them out also explains why the shield looks the way it does, and why a Bengals 7 and a Bills 7 are not the same object.

## 1. The brand typeface: Endzone

The league runs its communications on a proprietary family called Endzone. The NFL's own identity guidelines — the internal document Communicating the NFL Brand, which has circulated publicly for years — name three members: Endzone Sans, Endzone Slab and Endzone Tech. Endzone Slab is the headline face, reserved for titles and primary messaging. The guidelines credit it as bespoke type made for the National Football League by Village, the New York foundry run by Chester and Tracy Jenkins.

That attribution is worth sitting with, because Village is not a sports-graphics shop. It was a small, sharply curated type cooperative; the Jenkinses wound it into Constellation in 2011. The NFL went to a serious independent foundry for its wordmarks, and the work shows in ways a casual look misses — the slab is doing something more careful than "make it look tough."

Two things circulate about Endzone that do not hold up. The first is a specific launch year: some pages date Endzone Slab to 2013, while the font files themselves carry an NFL copyright from 2007 and the guidelines naming the family were already online by 2010. Those cannot all be right, and no authoritative source gives a date, so this piece gives none. The second is the claim that Endzone Tech is "based on Orbit." That one traces back to forum posts and font-download listings copying each other, with nothing from the NFL or from Village behind it. Treat it as unverified.

You cannot buy Endzone. It is licensed to the league's partners case by case and sold to nobody.

## 2. The shield is not type at all

The most common version of this question — what font is the NFL logo? — has an answer people don't like: it isn't one.

The shield is fixed artwork. The letters inside it are drawn, spaced and welded into the mark, and the NFL's guidelines treat the whole thing as a single asset that partners reproduce rather than rebuild. You cannot type NFL in any font and get the shield, and that is by design. It's the same principle as the Coca-Cola script and the Nike wordmark after 1995: at a certain level of recognition, a logo stops being set and starts being drawn, because a mark that can be retyped can be retyped badly.

Which does not stop the identification sites from naming a typeface anyway. Search the question and you will get confident, mutually contradictory answers — one page calls the shield's letters a custom serif, the next calls them a custom sans, a third names a specific Endzone weight. None cites the NFL. When three sources describing the same object disagree about whether it has serifs, the useful conclusion is that none of them looked.

The shield's last real change came in 2008, debuting at that year's draft. The star count dropped from 25 to eight, one per division, and the football was redrawn and tilted to echo the ball on the Vince Lombardi Trophy. The NFL's then-director of brand and creative operations, Jaime Weston, gave the cleanest possible justification at the time: after researching the shield's origins, the designers could find no reason for 25 stars.

> Twenty-five stars, for no reason anybody could reconstruct, for decades. Half of identity work is finding out which parts nobody can explain.

The letterforms were adjusted in that pass too. They have stayed put since.

## 3. The numbers are a different discipline entirely

Jersey numerals are the part people most often mean and the part with the least league-wide standardisation.

The rulebook governs the numbers, but only as measurements. Numerals must be at least 8 inches high on the front and 10 inches on the back, in a colour clearly contrasting with the shirt. That is the specification. What the digits actually look like — the weight, the width, whether the 4 is open or closed, whether the 1 gets a foot — is not in the rules. It belongs to the clubs and to Nike, which has been the league's on-field uniform supplier since 2012, when it took over from Reebok under a deal announced in 2010.

0 1 4 6 8
The digits that decide a numeral set. Shown in Vigil, not in any NFL numeral face.

So the honest answer to "what font are NFL numbers" is: thirty-two answers, several of them changed within the last decade, none of them released. A team that switches numeral styles is doing the same work a foundry does — redrawing a set of glyphs to a new brief — and the brief here is unusual. These characters get read at sixty miles an hour, from the far side of a stadium, on a compressed broadcast feed, wrapped around a moving body, often partly obscured, frequently wet.

That last constraint is the one designers underrate. A numeral on a jersey is never flat. It sits on a torso that twists, on fabric that stretches, and it is photographed from every angle including directly from the side. Counters that look generous on a flat proof close up when the shoulder rotates. This is why so many football numerals are wider and more open than they need to be on paper — the drawing has to survive being bent.

## The one NFL typeface you can actually read about

There is a fourth face here, and it is the best documented of the lot because a commercial foundry publishes it.

NFL Tackle was drawn by Miguel Reyes at Commercial Type in 2018, for NFL Network's rebrand by the design studio Trollbäck+Company. It is an all-caps sans in a single heavy weight, built for tight tracking and tight leading, with curves flattened on all sides.

That description reads like a list of restrictions, and it is. A single weight, no lowercase, designed to be set jammed together. Those constraints come straight from the job: a broadcast identity that lives in lower thirds, motion graphics and score bugs needs mass and a predictable rectangle, not a range. It is a typeface with almost no flexibility, which is precisely why it works where it works — and why it would be useless anywhere else.

## Why sports type leans heavy and condensed

Line up the answers above and a shared logic appears. Slab serifs for headlines. A single heavy weight for broadcast. Numerals fatter than they look like they need to be.

- Distance — everything is read further away than page type. Stroke weight survives distance; fine detail doesn't.

- Interference — stadium light, mud, motion blur, compression artefacts. Heavy strokes have margin to lose.

- Small sizes on bright grounds — a mark on a helmet, a bug in a corner. Light type on a bright field gets eaten by halation, the same optical problem that drove the American road-sign fight.

- Competition — sports graphics always share the frame with something moving. Type that doesn't assert itself disappears.

None of that is a style. It is four environmental constraints producing a family resemblance, the same way a stamping die produced the look of licence plates. The aesthetic came second.

## What a type designer takes from this

The interesting lesson is about range, and it runs against instinct.

A type designer's reflex is to build wide: more weights, more widths, italics, an axis from hairline to black. Coverage is how a family earns a place in a design system. The NFL's type does the opposite at every turn. Tackle has one weight and no lowercase. The shield has no typeface at all, only fixed artwork. The numerals are not a family — they are thirty-two small closed sets that never need to pair with anything.

What those decisions share is that each one is drawn for exactly one distance and one surface, and they give up everything else to be excellent there. That is a real strategy, and it is available to anyone willing to be honest about what a piece of lettering is for. Most type gets weaker as it gets more flexible.

The second lesson is about numerals, and it generalises well past football. Digits carry more load than letters and get a fraction of the attention. A misread word is usually recoverable from context; a misread number is just wrong. The pairs to check are always the same — 0 and O, 1 and l and I, 6 and 8, 3 and 8, 5 and S — and a football jersey is that test run at maximum difficulty: huge, moving, and consequential. Anyone drawing numerals for a dashboard, a scoreboard or a table should look at what survives on a torso.

Vigil is not a sports face and would be the wrong call for anything above. It is a geometric sans for interfaces and paragraphs, and a jersey needs something far heavier and more condensed than its widest setting. For that job, look at a proper athletic block, or at the free League Gothic for the broadcast-condensed look. What Vigil does share with the good numerals here is the discipline: tabular figures that hold their column, open counters, and a 1, l and I you can tell apart. That matters at reading distance too — just with less mud.

## The Nike font is Futura — with an asterisk — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/nike-font

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-09 — Keno Vigil

# The Nike font is Futura — with an asterisk

A 1927 German typeface, a logo that cost thirty-five dollars, and a slogan lifted from a man facing a firing squad.

NK

The Nike font is Futura. The NIKE wordmark that ran from 1978 to 1995 was set in Futura Bold — capitals, slanted forward, tucked into the Swoosh — and the company later licensed a bespoke cut of it. The asterisk is that Nike's logo has had no wordmark at all since 1995. The most valuable typography the brand owns is a shape with no letters in it.

This makes Nike the useful counter-example to Coca-Cola. Coke's logo is handwriting — a bookkeeper's Spencerian script from 1886, never a typeface, impossible to license. Nike's began with a font you can buy. Two of the most recognisable marks on earth, built the opposite way round.

## The $35 logo came first. The type came later.

The Swoosh was drawn in 1971 by Carolyn Davidson, then a graphic design student at Portland State University, where Phil Knight taught accounting. She was paid $35. It was registered as a trademark in June 1971 and appeared on shoes at the U.S. Olympic Trials in Eugene the following summer.

The $35 is the part everyone repeats, usually as a story about a company getting something for nothing. The rest of it gets left out: in 1983 Knight gave Davidson a gold Swoosh ring and 500 shares of Nike stock. She kept them.

Type was not part of that first mark. Through the early 1970s the Swoosh was paired with a lowercase cursive nike. The version people picture — solid Swoosh, hard capitals, the E running out into the Swoosh's tail — arrives in 1978, and that is where Futura enters.

## Futura, and the man the Gestapo came for

Futura was designed by Paul Renner and released by the Bauer Type Foundry in Frankfurt in 1927. It is the definitive geometric sans: circles for the round letters, straight lines for the stems, an alphabet assembled as though from a compass and a ruler.

Renner was not a Nazi sympathiser, which in 1930s Germany was a career. He published Kulturbolschewismus? — "Cultural Bolshevism?" — attacking the regime's cultural politics, and in 1933 he was arrested by the Gestapo and removed from his post running the Munich master school for printers.

The typeface outlived all of it. Futura is the only typeface to have reached the surface of the Moon: it is the type on the plaque the Apollo 11 crew left behind in 1969.

> A typeface drawn by a man the Gestapo arrested went to the Moon, and then sold running shoes. Type has a longer memory than the people who commission it.

So when a sportswear company in Oregon reached for a geometric sans in 1978, it was picking up something with a considerable amount of history already attached — none of which had anything to do with athletics.

## What "custom" actually means here

"Nike's font is custom" gets repeated a lot, usually without anyone saying what was customised. In this case there is something concrete to point at.

Neufville Digital — the foundry that holds and reissues the Bauer originals, Futura among them — publishes a family called Futura ND for Nike 365. It is a real, separately named release, listed in the type-reference literature and previously sold through retail channels. It is not available to the public now.

NIKE
Capitals, condensed, leaning forward. Shown in Vigil — not Futura, and not Nike's cut of it.

That is the ordinary shape of a large brand's relationship with type: license a classic, pay a foundry to cut a version fitted to your name, keep it. The wordmark was never Futura straight from the box. It was condensed, slanted, and spaced so that one letter could hand off into a logo.

## The claim nobody can actually source

Search for the Just Do It typeface and the internet will answer instantly and in unison. It should not.

Some sites say Futura Bold Condensed Oblique. Others say Futura Condensed Extra Black. They cannot both be right, and nearly all of them are font-download pages that exist to sell a lookalike — a category that copies from itself and rarely cites anything. Nike has published no specification. Wikipedia's article on the slogan reproduces the lettering and names no typeface at all.

What can be said honestly: it is a condensed, very heavy Futura, consistent with the family Nike already had cut for it. What cannot be said honestly is the exact weight, and the confident version of that answer is worth nothing.

This is the failure mode of "what font is that" as a genre. A guess gets published, the next site copies it, and repetition hardens into fact. It is the same mechanism that put a 2003 film-prop font in the history books as America's licence plate typeface.

## Where the line came from

The slogan is worth the detour, because its origin is genuinely dark and entirely on the record.

Dan Wieden, co-founder of Wieden+Kennedy in Portland, wrote Just Do It in 1988 for the campaign that launched that July. He has said publicly, more than once, that he took it from Gary Gilmore — the convicted murderer executed by firing squad in Utah in 1977, whose last words were "let's do it."

Wieden's account of the edit is characteristically dry: he did not like the "let's," and changing it meant he did not have to give Gilmore credit.

The commercial result is not in dispute. Between 1988 and 1998 Nike's share of the North American sport-shoe market went from 18% to 43%, and worldwide sales from roughly $877 million to $9.2 billion.

## Then they deleted the letters

The most interesting typographic decision Nike ever made was to stop using type.

In 1995 the word came off the logo. What remained was the Swoosh alone — no name, no wordmark, nothing to read. Very few companies can do this. It requires having spent two decades teaching the world to attach a name to a shape, and it only works once the teaching is finished.

Which reframes the whole question. People search for the Nike font expecting the answer to be the source of the brand's power. It isn't. The typography did its job and was then dismissed. Futura's role was to be legible, confident and slightly foreign for seventeen years while the Swoosh became the thing people actually recognised.

## What a type designer takes from this

Two things.

The first is that a logo is not a font, even when it is made of one. Futura Bold is a typeface; the Nike wordmark is a fixed drawing with a specific slant, specific spacing and one letter deliberately broken to meet a curve. Setting NIKE in Futura Bold on a computer does not reproduce the logo, and this is why "what font is that logo" so often has no clean answer. Wordmarks get frozen. Fonts stay flexible.

The second is about borrowed meaning. Futura in 1978 carried Bauhaus-era modernism, engineering, the Space Age — none of it about sport. Nike did not neutralise those associations. It used them: geometric type reads as precise and machine-made, and that is a useful thing to project onto a running shoe. Choosing a typeface is choosing a set of second-hand connotations and hoping they point where you need them to.

## What you can actually use

Futura is commercial. Neufville Digital licenses it as Futura ND, and the Nike cut is not for sale. Free files calling themselves the Nike font are either unlicensed Futura or hand-traced logos — and if the plan is to imitate Nike, the trademark problem arrives long before the font licence does.

If the goal is that geometric character with a licence you can live with, there are genuine options, and Vigil is not the closest of them. Vigil is not a Futura substitute and this piece is not going to pretend otherwise. Futura has a tiny lowercase, a single-storey a and a sharply pointed A — the things that make it look like 1927. Vigil has a large lowercase and a double-storey a, because it was drawn to be read in paragraphs rather than admired in headlines.

That difference is the recommendation. For a display line where the geometry is the point, use Futura and pay for it. For the eleven pages of copy behind that line — where Futura's small lowercase and wide spacing genuinely hurt — a geometric sans built for text will serve better. Vigil is free, under the SIL Open Font License, and drawn for exactly that job.

## Soft corners: a short history of the rounded sans — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/rounded-sans-history

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-08-21 — Keno Vigil

# Soft corners: a short history of the rounded sans

Kzl

Rounded terminals are older than type. Any letter painted with a brush or cut with a router ends in a curve, and signwriters have relied on that softness for as long as there have been shopfronts. In metal and phototype, though, rounding was a deliberate choice, and for most of the twentieth century it was a rare one.

The modern rounded sans is largely a product of the late 1970s. Helvetica Rounded appeared in 1978. A year later, Volkswagen commissioned a corporate face, and VAG Rounded — geometric bones, fully rounded ends — became one of the most recognisable brand typefaces of its era, later travelling well beyond the car company that named it. Arial Rounded followed the same recipe, and for two decades "rounded" meant exactly this: take a sans, round every terminal to the full stroke width, stop.

Screens changed the audience. Rounded sans faces read as friendly and approachable, which is why they became the default for consumer apps and children's products alike. Gotham Rounded, Nunito, Quicksand and Varela Round all arrived in the 2000s and 2010s, and the open-source ones spread everywhere Google Fonts did. Their shared weakness is the one VAG Rounded had: uniform rounding. Every corner is soft, so the I looks like a pill, the 1 loses its flag, and at text sizes the whole page goes slightly out of focus.

Vigil's answer is to ration the softness. Round where a stroke ends in open space and the eye reads it as a gesture. Round less where two strokes meet and the corner is doing structural work. Keep it to a minimum where recognition depends on a clean vertical — l, L, 1 and I take the softening, but only just enough to belong to the same alphabet. The result reads as a clean sans at 16px and only becomes visibly rounded at display sizes — the reverse of what most rounded fonts do, and the point of the whole exercise.

The underlying skeleton is a geometric one, which is a category with its own hundred-year argument behind it — that history is here, and the practical guide to spotting and choosing one is here.

## The Spotify font is Spotify Mix — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/spotify-font

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-14 — Keno Vigil

# The Spotify font is Spotify Mix

Eighteen months of work by a Berlin foundry, and a counter shaped like a transmitter. It replaced Circular — it is not a version of it, whatever the font blogs tell you.

pbd

Spotify uses Spotify Mix, a bespoke typeface launched in May 2024. It was drawn by the Berlin foundry Dinamo with Spotify's in-house creative team over roughly eighteen months, and it replaced Spotify Circular — the customised Circular the company had run on for years.

That last clause is where almost every other answer to this question goes wrong.

## The error worth correcting first

Search this question and you will repeatedly be told that Spotify Mix is "a custom variant of Circular with modified letterforms and spacing." It is not. Mix replaced Circular. It is a different typeface, by a different foundry, drawn from scratch.

The mistake is easy to reconstruct. Spotify genuinely did use a customised Circular, genuinely does now use something called Spotify Mix, and a site summarising both without checking dates will happily glue them into one sentence. Then the next site copies it. Within a year the invented version outnumbers the real one.

> This is the failure mode of the entire "what font is that" genre. Nobody checks. Everybody copies. A plausible sentence hardens into a fact.

It is the same mechanism that made a 2003 film-prop font into America's supposed licence plate typeface, and the reason no honest source will tell you the exact weight of the Nike "Just Do It" lettering.

## What came before: Circular, and the font of the 2010s

Circular was designed by Laurenz Brunner and published by the Swiss foundry Lineto. Spotify adopted a customised version of it during the mid-2010s and ran on it for the better part of a decade.

Circular is worth understanding because of how thoroughly it defined a period. A geometric sans with a large lowercase, tight even spacing and a friendly, slightly rounded feel, it became the house look of an entire cohort of technology companies — most famously Airbnb. For a stretch of years, "modern tech brand" and "Circular or something close to it" were nearly the same statement.

It earned that. Circular solved a real problem: it kept the clean geometry that reads as modern while enlarging the lowercase enough to survive a phone screen, which is exactly the compromise the older geometric faces refuse to make. It was warm without being cute, and it held up at interface sizes where stricter geometry falls apart.

Which is precisely the problem a company eventually runs into. A typeface you license is a typeface anyone can license.

## What Dinamo actually built

Spotify Mix is not a subtle refresh. The stated idea is mixing: it deliberately blends conventions from geometric, grotesque and humanist sans-serifs rather than committing to one genre, which is meant to echo the range of music and podcasts on the service.

The details that matter to a type designer:

- A transmitter shape in the counters. The enclosed negative space in letters like p, b and d is not a plain oval — it is shaped to suggest audio radiating outward. A brand metaphor buried inside the whitespace of a letter, where most people will never consciously notice it.

- A wide variable range, condensed through extended. Spotify's brand design lead framed this as emotional range: moving from condensed to extended lets the same words carry a different tone.

- Flicks and diagonal cuts on stroke terminals — the humanist inheritance, and what keeps it from reading as another neutral geometric sans.

- Alternates and multiple numeral sets, including plainer forms for moments when expressiveness is unwanted.

- Drawn for motion. It was built expecting to be animated, which is a design constraint that barely existed for typefaces twenty years ago.

p b d
The three letters where Mix hides its audio metaphor. Shown in Vigil, whose counters are plain open ovals and mean nothing at all.

## But the logo is a separate question

Plenty of people searching for the Spotify font do not want the interface typeface at all. They want the wordmark — the Spotify in the green.

That is its own object, and the general rule holds: a logotype is a fixed drawing, not a font. Once a wordmark is approved it stops being type and becomes artwork, with its spacing, proportions and any quirks frozen into a vector file. Setting the word in whatever typeface the brand uses elsewhere will not reproduce it, because the logo has been adjusted in ways no font can apply automatically.

So "what font is the Spotify logo" has the same answer as most versions of that question: none, exactly. It is lettering, drawn once and kept. The typeface question and the logo question look identical from a search box and are two entirely different things — which is a large part of why answers to both are so consistently muddled.

## Why a company builds its own typeface

Commissioning custom type is no longer exotic, and the reasoning is consistent.

Licensing at scale gets expensive and awkward. A retail licence covers a defined number of users, installs, page views. Multiply that across apps, web, television, out-of-home and dozens of markets, and the accounting becomes a standing obligation.

A licensed face carries no ownership. Circular was excellent and it was everywhere. There is no equity in looking like your competitors.

Off-the-shelf families rarely cover the range. A product surface needs a condensed weight for a cramped label, an extended one for a hero image, tabular numerals for durations, and the whole thing interpolating smoothly for animation. Commissioning that is often cheaper than assembling it from three families that disagree about proportion.

The contrast with Coca-Cola is instructive. Coke's identity is a piece of handwriting from 1886 that has barely moved. Spotify's is a variable font system with alternates, rebuilt from scratch after a decade. One brand's typography is a relic it protects; the other's is infrastructure it replaces.

## What a type designer takes from this

The interesting decision is not the drawing. It is the range.

Mix is built to be a toolbox rather than a voice: wide enough in width and weight that the same family can whisper or shout, with alternates for when the personality needs turning down. That is a genuinely different brief from the one most typefaces are drawn to. A text face wants to be consistent and invisible. A brand system increasingly wants to be a controllable instrument.

Variable font technology is what made that practical. Shipping condensed-through-extended as one interpolating file, rather than forty static cuts nobody installs correctly, is the difference between a system designers use and a system they route around.

The second thing worth noticing is that Mix's most distinctive feature is in the counters — the holes. Counters are where a typeface's character actually lives, far more than the outer silhouette, and they are the first thing to close up at small sizes or low contrast. Putting the brand idea there is a confident bet that the family will mostly be seen large.

## What you can actually use

Spotify Mix is proprietary. It is not sold, and it will not be. Circular can be licensed from Lineto, and it remains a genuinely good typeface. Anything offered as a free Spotify font download is an unlicensed copy of Circular, which is piracy with extra steps.

If what appeals is the category rather than the brand, plenty of geometric sans-serifs are free and legitimate. The field guide covers the options, and Vigil is one of them — a geometric sans with open counters and a large lowercase, free under the SIL Open Font License.

What Vigil will not do is imitate Spotify Mix, and it is worth saying plainly. Mix is a wide variable system with genre-mixing terminals and alternate sets, built by a commercial foundry over eighteen months for one company's specific surfaces. Vigil is a straight geometric sans for people who need good type and have no budget. Different problems. Reaching for a free font to imitate a bespoke one is the reliable way to end up with something that looks like a near-miss, and a near-miss reads worse than an honest difference.

## The Stranger Things font is ITC Benguiat — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/stranger-things-font

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-06 — Keno Vigil

# The Stranger Things font is ITC Benguiat

Drawn in 1977, twenty years before the show is set to remember it. The brief was twelve Stephen King paperbacks in a padded envelope.

1977

It's ITC Benguiat — a decorative serif drawn by Ed Benguiat and released by the International Typeface Corporation in 1977. The title treatment stretches its serifs and tightens the fit, so what you see on screen is a customised setting rather than the typeface straight from the box. But the bones, and all of the feeling, are Benguiat's.

## The brief was a stack of paperbacks

When the Duffer Brothers briefed the title sequence, they didn't describe a typeface. They sent twelve vintage Stephen King book covers and asked for that style and that feeling.

That is a better brief than most typographers ever get, because it specifies the association rather than the artefact. It doesn't say "serif, condensed, glowing red." It says: make me feel the thing I felt looking at a rack of paperbacks in 1983.

The studio that answered it was Imaginary Forces, with creative director Michelle Dougherty. What they found when they went looking through those covers was that a single face kept recurring — because ITC Benguiat had been all over King's 1980s editions. The show didn't borrow a mood and then find a font. It followed the mood back to the font that had been generating it all along.

## Why a 1977 typeface says "1983" so well

ITC Benguiat is loosely based on Art Nouveau letterforms, though it is explicitly not an academic revival — Benguiat took the flavour of the period, the swelling curves and the high waistline, and drew something that had never actually existed. It is a 1970s idea of an older thing.

That double distance is exactly why it works. The show is a 2016 idea of the 1980s, whose paperbacks were a 1980s idea of the 1970s, whose type was a 1970s idea of 1900. Nostalgia stacked four deep, and it reads as authentic because each layer was sincere when it was made.

There is a lesson in that for anyone reaching for a retro face. The reason Benguiat evokes the era isn't that it looks old. It's that it looks like a specific era's taste in looking old.

## The sequence is doing something harder than it looks

The title itself is close to still. Letters drift in from the edges, red on black, and lock into place while the synthesiser climbs. There is no camera move to hide behind, no imagery, nothing happening but type assembling itself.

Dougherty has described the work as concentrating on the type and finding the most beautiful combinations of it — which sounds modest and is not. A sequence with nothing in it but letterforms has nowhere to put a weak decision. Every frame is the typeface, so every frame is either working or exposed.

What the drift buys is unease. The letters begin disjointed, slightly wrong, not yet a word, and the resolution into STRANGER THINGS arrives as relief a half-second before the music confirms it. That is a typographic effect, not a cinematic one. The tension comes from withholding legibility and then granting it.

It is also the reason the logo survives outside the sequence. Because the treatment is nearly the typeface itself — extended serifs, tight fit, no illustration — it still reads on a phone icon, a T-shirt, a birthday cake. Title designs that lean on effects usually don't travel. This one is just letters, and letters travel.

## You have been reading it your whole life

Once you can see ITC Benguiat you cannot stop. It is on the 1980s Stephen King covers, obviously. It is also on the Choose Your Own Adventure books, which means an entire generation absorbed it before they could name a typeface at all. It is on The Smiths' Strangeways, Here We Come. It runs through Quentin Tarantino's title sequences, including the cast names in Pulp Fiction. It has appeared in Star Trek film titles.

That is a strange career for a piece of lettering: children's gamebooks, horror paperbacks, an English guitar band, and a director who quotes the seventies on purpose. The common thread isn't genre. It's that all of them wanted to feel like a slightly disreputable memory.

## The man who drew it

Ed Benguiat, 1927 to 2020, drew more than six hundred typefaces. Tiffany, Bookman, Souvenir, Edwardian Script, and the Benguiat family that carries his name. He was central to the founding of the International Typeface Corporation, the first independent licensing company for type designers, and worked with Herb Lubalin on U&lc, the magazine that taught a generation of designers what type could do.

He died on 15 October 2020, aged 92, which means he lived to watch a typeface he had drawn forty-three years earlier become the visual signature of one of the most-watched shows on television. Not many designers get that. Most typefaces that end up defining a decade do it long after the person who drew them has stopped being able to enjoy it.

> Six hundred typefaces, and the one everybody knows is the one that spells a town in Indiana that doesn’t exist.

## What the letters are actually doing

Strip the red glow and look at the drawing. ITC Benguiat is high-contrast for a display serif — thick stems against hairline-ish thins — with a waistline pushed unusually high, so the crossbar of the E and the joint of the R sit above the optical centre. That is the Art Nouveau inheritance, and it is what gives the face its slightly stretched, top-heavy poise.

The serifs are the signature. They are not the crisp wedges of a Times or the slabs of a Rockwell; they flare, curving out of the stem rather than meeting it at an angle. In the show's treatment they are extended further still, which is the one real intervention — pull those flares out and the letters start to interlock, which is why the logo reads as a single object rather than fourteen characters.

It is also, honestly, a difficult face. That high waist and heavy contrast make it uncomfortable below about thirty pixels, and the flared serifs clog at small sizes. ITC Benguiat is a poster face wearing a book face's serifs, and it should be treated as one. The people who set body copy in it because they liked the show are finding this out.

## Can you download it?

Not for free, not legitimately. ITC Benguiat is a commercial typeface and is licensed through its publisher. The results promising a free Stranger Things font are, with few exceptions, either unlicensed copies of Benguiat's work or loose imitations drawn to resemble it — and the imitations tend to fall apart exactly where the original is doing its best work, at the serif joins and the terminals.

If you need the real thing for a real project, buy the licence. It is a hundred-year-old idea drawn by a master and it is still earning its keep; paying for it is not a hardship.

If you want the feeling without the licence, look for openly licensed faces with genuine Art Nouveau bones rather than a Benguiat knock-off. You will get something honest instead of something that will look wrong at large sizes and get your project a takedown notice.

## What a type designer takes from this

The Stranger Things logo is often held up as great type design. It isn't, quite — it's great type selection, which is a different and in some ways harder skill.

Nobody drew new letterforms to make you feel 1983. Someone recognised that the feeling already lived inside a forty-year-old typeface, and had the discipline to use it nearly straight, stretch the serifs, and get out of the way. The work was in the looking.

That is the part worth stealing. A typeface arrives carrying everywhere it has already been — every paperback, every album sleeve, every gamebook a nine-year-old read under a duvet. You cannot draw that in. You can only find it, and then decide whether the baggage is the thing you want.

Which is also the argument for knowing what category a face belongs to before you pick it. Vigil is a geometric sans and carries geometric baggage: Bauhaus, modernity, confidence, a certain coolness. It would be a terrible choice for a horror title, and no amount of good drawing would fix that.

## Typeface vs font: the distinction that stopped mattering in 1985 — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/typeface-vs-font

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-04 — Keno Vigil

# Typeface vs font: the distinction that stopped mattering in 1985

It was a real difference once, and it described a real object. Here is what it meant, and why almost nobody needs to keep score.

Aa

A typeface is the design. A font is the thing you set it with. Garamond is a typeface. Ten-point Garamond Italic, as a drawer full of metal, was a font. That distinction was precise, useful and physical for about four hundred years, and then digital type quietly dissolved the reason for it.

## Where the words came from

“Font” comes from the French fonte — something melted, something cast. That is exactly what it was. A punchcutter cut each character at a specific size, a matrix was struck from it, and molten metal was cast into that matrix. The output was a physical set of sorts: every letter, numeral and mark you needed, at one size, in one style.

So a font was inventory. If a print shop owned Caslon in 10-point roman, 10-point italic and 12-point roman, it owned three fonts of one typeface. Wanting the same design a little larger meant buying more metal, because there was no way to scale a piece of lead.

The typeface, meanwhile, was the design itself — the decisions a punchcutter made about how an a should be shaped. It existed across every size, and it belonged to whoever drew it.

> A typeface is what you see. A font is what you use.

## What broke it

Phototypesetting came first, in the 1950s and 60s, projecting characters from film through a lens. One filmstrip could now be enlarged or reduced, so a single “font” covered a range of sizes for the first time. The link between a font and one specific size was already loosening.

Then PostScript arrived in 1984, the Apple LaserWriter shipped in 1985, and type became mathematics. An outline described by curves scales to any size at all. The physical object the word “font” had named for four centuries — the case of metal at one size — simply stopped existing.

What replaced it was a file. And because the file is the thing you buy, install, license and email to a printer, “font” attached itself to the file, and then, inevitably, to the design inside it.

## What the words mean now

TypefaceThe design. The intellectual work — the shapes, proportions and rules that make Futura recognisably Futura at any size.

FontThe file that delivers the design. In practice also the common word for the design itself, which is not an error so much as a change.

Font familyAll the related styles that share one design: the weights, their italics, and any extra widths or variants.

WeightHow heavy the strokes are — Light, Regular, Bold, Black. Usually numbered 100 to 900.

StyleRoman or italic. A true italic is drawn separately, not slanted by software.

Variable fontOne file containing a continuous range rather than fixed steps. This is where the old distinction quietly returns.

GlyphOne drawn shape in the file. Distinct from a character: “fi” is one glyph and two characters.

## A worked example

Vigil is one typeface. Its family contains eight weights from ExtraLight to Black, each with a matching italic — sixteen styles — plus a separate Outline style in roman and italic.

Shipped as individual files, that is twenty fonts. Shipped as variable fonts, it is two: one roman file and one italic file, each carrying the entire 200–900 weight axis as a continuous range. Same typeface, same family, same eighteen styles. Two files or twenty, depending on how you want to load it.

That sentence is only sayable because the words still mean different things. It is also the clearest case for keeping both of them around.

## When it still matters

- Licensing. You license fonts, not typefaces. A licence usually grants a specific number of installations of specific files, which is why the file is the unit that counts. In most jurisdictions the letterform designs themselves are far harder to protect than the software that draws them.

- Production. “Send me the font” means send the file. “Which typeface is this?” means name the design. Asking the wrong one gets you the wrong answer.

- Variable fonts. Once a single file spans a hundred weights, “font” means something genuinely distinct from any one of the designs inside it.

## The verdict

The distinction is real, and it is worth understanding if you work with type, because it explains why licences are shaped the way they are and why a family can be two files or twenty.

It is not worth correcting people over. The word “font” absorbed the broader meaning because the object it originally named stopped existing, and language does that. Anyone who says “I love this font” is being understood perfectly. Where it matters — a licence, a handoff, an invoice — say which one you mean and move on.

## There is no VHS font — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/vhs-font

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-14 — Keno Vigil

# There is no VHS font

Three different things go by that name, and only one of them has a typeface as the answer. The other two are a chip and a broken signal.

PLAY

"VHS font" is three questions wearing one coat. The VHS logo is set in Lee, a 1970s typeface by Leo Weisz. The blocky on-screen text from a VCR was never a typeface at all — it was a bitmap baked into a chip. And the VHS look people actually want is mostly not typography.

Sort out which one you mean and the answer becomes easy. Fail to, and you end up with crisp retro lettering that stubbornly refuses to look like a tape.

## The logo: Lee, by Leo Weisz, 1976

The VHS wordmark — the tall, tightly packed capitals with those distinctive flat-sided curves — was produced in 1976 for the Victor HR-3300, the first VCR to use the format. It is set in Lee, a typeface drawn by Leo Weisz for Visual Graphics Corporation.

Lee is a very 1970s object: dense, geometric, slightly claustrophobic, built for photo-lettering rather than metal. The same face was used for the Charlie's Angels title sequence the same year. Weisz, by the accounts of people who track this, lived past a hundred and kept working.

> One typeface, one year, two artefacts that now function as shorthand for the entire decade. 1976 was a good year for Leo Weisz.

Lee also explains why the logo is so hard to reproduce by setting it. Photo-lettering faces of that era were drawn to be manipulated — stretched, tightened, overlapped on the film — and the VHS wordmark takes full advantage, with the three letters packed far closer than any default spacing would allow. Type it out in Lee and you get something recognisably related and visibly not the logo.

This is the only part of the question with a clean typographic answer, and it is the part almost nobody is asking about.

## The on-screen text: a chip, not a font

What people usually mean by "the VHS font" is the chunky white lettering a VCR painted over the picture. PLAY. REC. STOP. 12:00.

That was never type in any sense a foundry would recognise. It came from the machine's on-screen display circuit, which held a font ROM — a small read-only memory storing each character as a grid of dots. The circuit decoded a position, pulled the matching bit pattern, and painted it into the video signal during the blanking interval between scan lines.

So the letters were not drawn by a type designer and licensed. They were drawn by an engineer, on graph paper, to fit a dot matrix and a memory budget. Different manufacturers shipped different character sets. Different models from the same manufacturer often did too.

## Why it looks like that

Every feature of that lettering is a consequence of the job, in the same way that licence plate letters were shaped by a stamping die.

- Coarse and blocky because a character was a handful of dots across. There was no resolution for a curve, so curves became staircases.

- Monospaced because a character generator addresses a fixed grid. Proportional spacing needs arithmetic the chip was not going to do.

- Heavy strokes because thin ones vanish on an interlaced display, where alternate scan lines refresh on alternate fields and a one-pixel horizontal flickers.

- Outlined or drop-shadowed because the text sits on top of arbitrary video. White on white is unreadable, so the characters carry their own contrast with them.

- Widely spaced because analogue bandwidth smears horizontal detail, and letters set tight would bleed into each other.

Not one of those is a style decision. The aesthetic that now signals nostalgia was a set of grudging compromises with a cheap chip and a noisy signal.

## The font everyone actually downloads

If you want that look as type, the answer in practice is VCR OSD Mono, released in 2014 by Riciery Santos Leal. It is a monospaced bitmap-style font emulating vintage VCR on-screen display text, free for personal and commercial use, and it has been downloaded several million times.

It is worth being precise about what it is. VCR OSD Mono is a homage, not a digitisation — it was drawn to evoke the category, not traced from one manufacturer's character ROM. That is not a criticism. There is no canonical original to be faithful to, because every machine had its own.

PLAY ▮ 12:00
The two strings that carry the whole reference. Shown in Vigil, which is a completely wrong choice for this and is here to make the point.

## The part the font will not fix

Here is where most VHS-styled work goes wrong. Set VCR OSD Mono cleanly, in white, on a flat background, and it does not read as VHS. It reads as a pixel font.

The VHS signature is not in the letterforms. It is in the degradation:

- Chroma bleed — colour carried at far lower bandwidth than brightness, so saturated edges smear sideways, especially reds and magentas.

- Scan lines and interlacing, with the comb artefacts that appear on anything moving.

- Tracking error — the torn horizontal band that shudders up the frame.

- Generation loss, the softness and noise of a copy of a copy.

Those are signal properties, not typographic ones. A designer chasing the VHS look with font choice alone is solving maybe a fifth of the problem. The other four fifths are a chroma-offset filter and a willingness to make things look broken.

## Building the look, in the right order

If the goal is a convincing tape, the typography is the last step rather than the first. A workable order:

- Start at 4:3. Nothing reads as VHS in a widescreen frame. The aspect ratio does more work than any filter.

- Set the text in a monospaced bitmap face, in white, with a hard black outline or shadow. Keep it in the corners — top left for the mode, bottom for the counter — because that is where a real machine put it, and placement is a stronger cue than letterform.

- Only then degrade. Chroma offset first, pushing red and blue apart horizontally by a pixel or two. Then scan lines. Then a little noise and softness.

- Break something. One tracking band, one dropout, one moment of instability. Perfect degradation is a contradiction, and evenly-applied grain reads as a filter rather than as damage.

- Resist the urge to be legible. The reference depends on the picture being slightly worse than you are comfortable shipping.

The common failure is applying a heavy filter to everything uniformly, including the overlay text. On a real machine the character generator painted after the tape was read, so the on-screen text was noticeably cleaner than the footage under it. Degrading them equally is the tell that something was made in software.

## What a type designer takes from this

Two things, and the first is now a running theme on this site.

Constraints become styles once the constraints are gone. Nobody in 1985 thought the VCR character generator was attractive. It was what fit in the chip. Forty years later, the marks left by that limitation are the entire point — exactly as happened with embossed plate lettering, which is now reproduced by flat printers that never met a die. A constraint that leaves a visible fingerprint will eventually be imitated by people who have no idea what caused it.

The second is about where meaning lives. If the feeling you want comes from degradation, no typeface will deliver it, because typefaces are drawn clean. This is a genuinely useful diagnostic: when a reference will not come together, ask whether the thing you are copying is the shape or the damage. Half the time it is the damage, and then you need a filter, not a font.

## Vigil is the wrong tool here, obviously

No hedging required. Vigil is a clean geometric sans with smooth curves and open counters, drawn for screens that render accurately. It has nothing to offer a project that wants to look like a worn tape, and dressing it up with a glitch filter would be a costume rather than a reference.

Use VCR OSD Mono for the on-screen text. Track down Lee if you need the logo, and expect to draw the wordmark rather than set it. Then spend your effort on the signal, because that is where the effect actually lives.

Vigil is for the other part — the legible geometric sans that carries the words around the reference. It is free under the SIL Open Font License, and it is honest about not being a time machine.
