## Why a serif, and why Vollkorn — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/vigil-serif

Vigil
Try itWeightsSerifNotesDownload

2026-09-18 — Keno Vigil

# Why a serif, and why Vollkorn.

a

Vigil shipped as a sans and nothing else. A text sans that disappears at 16px and shows its personality at 96 was the whole brief. Set real things in it — a long article, a set of release notes, a page of documentation — and you run into the thing every sans-only system runs into. There is no second voice. Every quote, every aside, every footnote has to be signalled with size or weight or color, because the typeface itself only has one register.

Italics help. They are not enough. An italic is a change of tone inside a sentence; what long-form writing wants is a change of material between blocks. Body copy in one family, interface in another. That's the oldest layout convention there is, and it exists because it works.

## The problem with pairing

The usual fix is to pair your sans with someone else's serif. The candidates are not the problem; the arithmetic is. Two typefaces drawn by two people at two different times almost never share an x-height, and they never share a line box. So you spend your afternoon nudging: serif at 17.5 to match the sans at 17, one family's line-height at 1.6 and the other at 1.52, a negative margin on the pull quote because its cap sits four pixels high.

> Every one of those nudges is a decision that should have been made once, in the font, instead of a thousand times, in the CSS.

So the goal stopped being "find a serif that looks nice beside Vigil" and became "make a serif that measures the same as Vigil." Same cap height. Same x-height. Same descender. Same line box. Drop it in at the same size on the same baseline and nothing moves.

## Why Vollkorn

Vigil Serif is not drawn from scratch, for the same reason Vigil itself is not: the alphabet is not the hard part. What it needed was a skeleton with the right temperament, released under a license that lets you rebuild it.

Friedrich Althausen's Vollkorn is that. It was first published in 2005, one of the first genuinely good free serifs, it has been maintained and expanded for twenty years, and it carries about 2,300 glyphs across Latin, Cyrillic and Greek — a range it would take me years to draw and longer to kern. Critically, it isn't precious. It's a warm, sturdy, slightly rustic bread-and-butter serif; the name means "wholegrain." It was built to be read in long stretches, which is exactly the job.

It also had the one quality I couldn't manufacture: it doesn't fight a geometric sans. A high-contrast Didone beside Vigil looks like a costume change. Vollkorn's moderate contrast and open counters sit next to a large-x-height geometric sans without either one shouting.

Vigil Serif, 300 — the stem-matched pairing

Handgloves & bibliography

Serif at 300 and sans at 400 share a stem.

## What reproportioning actually means

This is the part I underestimated. Matching another typeface's metrics is not a scale factor. Vollkorn's proportions are its own: relative to Vigil the x-height sits differently against the caps, and the ascenders don't stop where Vigil's do. Scaling the whole thing until the x-heights agree gives you caps that are too tall, a descender that's too deep, and a line box that no longer matches — you've traded one mismatch for three.

So the work was structural, one horizontal at a time. Set the cap height to Vigil's. Pull the x-height up until the ratio matches — Vigil's is 0.714, and that number is the whole reason the two look like relatives rather than neighbors. Bring the ascenders down to stop flat on the cap line, as Vigil's do, so caps and lowercase share one ceiling. Hold the descender at Vigil's depth. Then rebuild the vertical metrics so the line box lands on 1.200 em, identical to the sans.

What I deliberately did not do is squeeze the widths. The serif sets about six percent wider than Vigil in lowercase, and it should: that extra width is the serifs. Forcing it to Vigil's set width would mean narrowing the skeleton to make room for the brackets, which is how you get a serif that looks starved. Six percent is the honest cost of the serifs, and it's small enough that a paragraph reflows by a word or two rather than a line or two.

One consequence worth knowing, because it will bite anyone who pairs them: at the same nominal weight, the serif reads heavier. Serifs add ink at every terminal. So the stem-matched pairing is serif 300 beside sans 400 — the serif steps down one stop to look like it weighs the same.

## What it's for, and what it isn't

Content. Articles, documentation, books, quotes, footnotes, tables of figures where old-style numerals keep the column quiet. Above roughly fourteen pixels it is a better reading face than the sans, and the italic is a real italic with its own drawings, not a slant.

Not interface. Below fourteen pixels the serifs thicken into the counters and dense rows stop scanning; tracked-out all-caps navigation pulls the serifs apart until each word reads as separate marks. The division I've settled on is the simplest one available: content in the serif, interface in the sans.

## Where it stands

Version 1.100: variable roman and italic on one axis from 200 to 900, and sixteen hinted statics. Small caps, old-style, lining and tabular figures, fractions, superscripts and subscripts all work. It is free under the SIL Open Font License, like the sans, because Vollkorn was free under it first. That's not generosity on anyone's part; it's the license doing exactly what it was written to do, twice.

Go look at it and tell me what breaks.

— Keno Vigil, Cary, North Carolina

## The Constitution isn’t written in a font — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/what-font-is-the-constitution-written-in

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-19 — Keno Vigil

# The Constitution isn’t written in a font

A clerk, a quill and a weekend. Two different hands on one sheet of parchment, and neither of them is type.

We

The Constitution is not written in a font. It is handwriting — engrossed on parchment by Jacob Shallus, assistant clerk of the Pennsylvania General Assembly, who wrote roughly 4,500 words over a weekend in September 1787 and was paid $30. The body is eighteenth-century round hand. The We the People heading is something else entirely.

That second sentence is where the search results usually stop and where the interesting part starts. Most pages answering this question treat the document as if it had one look. It has two, they come from two different traditions, and they may not even be by the same person.

## What “engrossed” actually means

The word is everywhere in eighteenth-century records and almost nowhere outside archives now. To engross a document is to produce the final, formal, fair copy — the one that gets signed. Not a draft, not a printing. One physical object, written out by hand in a script chosen for occasion rather than speed.

The Convention voted on the Constitution on 15 September 1787 and adjourned so it could be engrossed and printed. Delegates signed on the seventeenth. The gap is one working weekend, and Shallus filled it.

Consider it as a production job. Four sheets of parchment — animal skin, limed and stretched, following English legal practice. A quill cut from a large feather. Ink of oak galls, iron and gum arabic, which bites into the surface rather than sitting on it. No undo. Thirty-nine men are going to sign the bottom of it in forty-eight hours.

## The body: round hand

The script Shallus used for the text is round hand — the standard clerical and business hand of the eighteenth-century English-speaking world, learned from engraved copybooks. American clerks typically worked from George Fisher or George Bickham; Bickham's The Universal Penman, published in 1743, was the most celebrated of them.

Round hand is the ancestor of the looping cursive taught in American schools. It is not the same thing, and it is emphatically not Spencerian, the flashier nineteenth-century business hand that produced the Coca-Cola wordmark. Spencerian did not exist in 1787. Any page that describes the Constitution as written in Spencerian script is off by about half a century.

We the People
Shown in Vigil, not in round hand. The point of the comparison is how little a geometric sans has in common with a quill.

What separates round hand from a typeface is not elegance. It is variation. The stroke swells and thins because a cut quill does that under pressure, and the pressure changes with the pull. Letters connect differently depending on what precedes them. A typeface is a set of repeatable parts; a hand is a performance, and the performance leaves evidence.

## The heading: yes, that part really is blackletter

Here is the correction worth making, because it runs both ways.

People look at the Constitution, register something spiky and archaic, and say “Old English.” Type-minded people then correct them: no, it's cursive, it's a hand, there's no blackletter in it. The confident correction is wrong.

The large display words — We the People, and the Article headings — are drawn in an engrossed gothic style based on the German Text and Square Text exemplars in Bickham's copybooks. That is blackletter. Keith Bates of the Manchester foundry K-Type, who extrapolated a digital typeface called We The People directly from those letters, classifies the result as blackletter, and the classification is not a stretch.

So the honest answer to “is the Constitution in Old English?” is: the headings are, the text isn't, and the page deliberately mixes two lettering traditions. Formal script for the body, gothic display for the parts that had to shout. An art-direction decision, made in 1787, by a clerk working overnight.

> One parchment, two alphabets, forty-eight hours. Whoever laid it out was thinking about hierarchy, not just handwriting.

## The son theory

Arthur Plotnik's The Man Behind the Quill: Jacob Shallus, Calligrapher of the United States Constitution — published by the National Archives in 1987, the bicentennial year, and still the only book-length study of the man — raises a possibility that has stuck.

Plotnik suggests the calligraphic headings may have been inserted by someone else: Shallus's teenage son Francis, later a working engraver. The evidence is compositional, not documentary. The Article headings are squeezed awkwardly into the spaces Shallus left for them, in a way that suggests a second hand filling gaps — and not an especially experienced one.

Label it for what it is: a scholar's inference from the artefact, repeated online far more confidently than Plotnik put it. Nobody knows who drew We the People. That the question is open at all is the useful part.

## The mistakes are still on it

The most human thing about the document is that it is visibly corrected.

Above the signatures sits an errata note, written into the engrossment itself, listing the fixes: “The Word, ‘the,’ being interlined between the seventh and eighth Lines of the first Page, The Word ‘Thirty’ being partly written on an Erazure in the fifteenth Line of the first Page, The Words ‘is tried’ being interlined between the thirty second and thirty third Lines of the first Page…” You can read the whole thing in the National Archives transcription, where it appears exactly where Shallus put it.

A scraped word. Three interlineations. All of it declared in the text, because on a signed instrument an unexplained alteration is worse than a visible one. The founding document of the United States ships with a changelog.

## The printed Constitution is a separate question

If the question is really “what type was the Constitution set in,” that has an answer, and it isn't the parchment.

John Dunlap and David Claypoole printed the official edition in Philadelphia and ran the text in The Pennsylvania Packet and Daily Advertiser on 19 September 1787, two days after the signing. It was set in Caslon.

Caslon is also what Dunlap used for the broadside of the Declaration of Independence on the night of 4 July 1776. Two founding documents, one printing house, one English typeface — William Caslon's, cut in London. The revolution was announced in the type of the country it was seceding from, which is either an irony or a supply-chain fact depending on how romantic you are feeling.

Be precise about what that does not mean. Caslon was not chosen. It was the roman a good Philadelphia shop had in its cases. The association came afterwards, and it is strong enough now that Caslon reads as American-founding to people who have never heard of William Caslon.

## Fonts that imitate it, and what they can’t do

Two are worth knowing, and it matters which document each one comes from.

- We The People, by Keith Bates at K-Type — drawn from the Constitution's own engrossed heading, by way of the Bickham models behind it. The backslanted original is free for personal, educational and charitable use; upright versions are licensed. This is the closest thing to a Constitution font that exists.

- American Scribe, by Brian Willson at Three Islands Press — based on Timothy Matlack's hand on the engrossed Declaration of Independence, not on Shallus's. Different scribe, different document, eleven years earlier. It gets lumped in constantly; it is a Declaration face.

Both are good work and both hit the same wall. A revival of a hand has to pick one version of each letter and then repeat it. The original never repeated anything. OpenType alternates and contextual substitution soften that — American Scribe ships a lot of both — but set a long passage in either and the eye starts finding the loop: the same e, at the same angle, forever. Real handwriting never gives you that, which is exactly why it reads as real.

Check anything below those two before trusting it. Search “Constitution font” and most of what returns is download aggregators reposting each other's files and each other's history — telling you the document is Spencerian, or Old English, or the work of Thomas Jefferson. Jefferson drafted the Declaration. He wrote out neither document for signing, and he was in Paris during the Convention.

## What a type designer takes from this

Three things, and the first is the oldest lesson in the trade.

Hierarchy predates typography. Shallus — or whoever drew those headings — had no size palette, no weight axis, no second family to switch to. What he had was a different alphabet, and he used it the way a designer today uses a display cut: to mark the entrance. The instinct to make the opening words behave differently from the body is older than movable type and it has never needed a style sheet.

Second: irregularity is information. Round hand carries the pressure of the pen and the speed of the hand, and a reader picks that up without naming it. Digital type deleted the variation and has spent decades buying pieces of it back — contextual alternates, randomised ligatures, variable axes. All approximations of something the quill got for free, and none of them solved.

Third, and most practical: the question “what font is that?” is often the wrong question. It assumes every piece of lettering was chosen from a menu. Plenty of the most recognisable lettering in the world wasn't — not the Constitution, not the Coca-Cola script, not most logos. Asking what font it is skips the more useful question of who made those marks, with what tool, under what deadline. In this case the answer is: a clerk, a quill, and a weekend.

Vigil is the wrong typeface for anything on this page, and it is worth saying plainly. It is a geometric sans built for screens and paragraphs — circular bowls, even strokes, no calligraphic memory at all. Set the preamble in it and you get a competent, completely ahistorical block of text. For period work use a real revival: a Caslon for the printed documents, We The People for the heading, a proper roundhand for the body. Then set your own writing in something that belongs to your own century.

## A vigil is what you keep when you refuse to go to sleep on something — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/why-vigil

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-04 — Keno Vigil

# A vigil is what you keep when you refuse to go to sleep on something.

K.

For more than ten years there was a calendar block on my phone that said MAKE FONT. All caps. Recurring. Set to “free,” which is calendar-speak for this will not happen today either. I started three times. Maybe four. A sketchbook of lowercase a’s here, a half-drawn alphabet there, a folder called font_final_v2 that I’m not going to open in front of you. Every start died the same way: I got the letters I loved and then met the four hundred glyphs I didn’t, and I went back to my actual job.

My actual job, for fifteen years, has been building software for people who don’t have time for bad software. Nurses studying at 11pm. Doctors trying to learn a procedure between patients. Clinical trials that live or die on a form. That work teaches you one thing above everything else: nobody is going to admire your interface. They’re going to read it, fast, tired, on a phone, and either understand or not. Typography isn’t decoration in that world. It’s the whole product wearing a disguise.

So I always knew what I wanted. Not a display face, not a logo with pretensions. A text face. Something you could set a paragraph in at sixteen pixels and forget about, and then blow up to 200 pixels and go, oh. Oh, that’s got a personality.

## Where the taste comes from

I grew up in Parsippany, New Jersey, which is to say I grew up reading highway signs, and then in Morehead City, North Carolina, which is to say I grew up reading the sides of boats. Both taught me the same lesson: letters that have to work outdoors, at speed, for strangers, are the honest ones. Geometric bones. Big x-height. No tricks.

Then came the fonts I actually fell for. Gotham’s confidence. Avenir’s quiet intelligence, the way it looks mathematical and isn’t. Montserrat, which taught a whole generation of us what a free font could be. And the rounded ones, which I loved and didn’t trust, because most rounded fonts are just regular fonts that got a little too friendly at the party.

The thing I wanted didn’t exist: a geometric grotesk with the softness applied like an engineer would apply it. On purpose. In specific places. With a rule.

## Rounded by rule, not by default

That became the whole design. Vigil rounds most at the exposed terminals, the ends of the C and S and the arms of the E, where a stroke stops and the eye lands. It rounds less at the structural corners. It doesn’t round the punctuation at all, because a period should still be a period.

> Soften where you meet people. Stay square where the structure needs you. Don’t blur the periods.

I have come to believe this is also a decent way to live.

## Why it finally shipped

Two things changed.

The first is that in June I climbed the height of Everest on a ski hill in Utah over 36 hours, one lap at a time, because I’d signed up for it and the date came. I had also, at some point before that, run a marathon for the same reason. The lesson was not inspiring. It was procedural. Things get finished when the finish line is on the calendar as a fact instead of a wish.

The second is that I stopped pretending a font has to be born from nothing. Every typeface is a fork of the alphabet. Vigil is built on Figtree, Erik Kennedy’s open-source geometric sans, under a license that exists precisely so people like me can take a great skeleton and give it a different body. I didn’t draw every curve from scratch. I decided what every curve should be, which turns out to be the part I’d been avoiding for ten years. The rest is code, patience, and a lot of squinting at the letter K.

It shipped on September 4, 2026. Eight weights, italics, an outline for when you want to shout, and a variable axis that goes from whisper to wall. It is free. It will always be free. No email, no account, no “just tell us where you work.” Download the zip.

## What Vigil means

It’s my name, sure. But the word came first. A vigil is staying awake through the long stretch when nothing is happening yet, because you’ve decided something will.

Ten years is a long vigil. Turns out you can keep one and still finish.

Now go set something in it.

— Keno Vigil, Cary, North Carolina

## The worst fonts, by someone who makes fonts — Vigil

https://www.vigilfont.com/notes/worst-fonts

Vigil
Try itWeightsNotesUse itDownload

2026-09-07 — Keno Vigil

# The worst fonts, by someone who makes fonts

The famous villains are competent typefaces with sincere origin stories. The genuinely bad ones fail at things nobody argues about on the internet.

?!

Almost every font on almost every worst-fonts list is fine. Comic Sans, Papyrus, Curlz, Brush Script — these are competently drawn typefaces that got put to work in places they were never designed for, and then took the blame for the person who put them there. The genuinely bad ones are boring, and nobody argues about them.

I want to defend the famous ones first, because the defence explains what actually makes type bad.

## Comic Sans was made for a product it missed

Vincent Connare designed Comic Sans at Microsoft, released in October 1994. He made it for Microsoft Bob, a piece of software with a cartoon dog that spoke to you in speech bubbles — and which, when Connare saw it, was setting those speech bubbles in Times New Roman. A cartoon dog talking to you in the typeface of the London Times. He was right that this was wrong.

He had The Dark Knight Returns, lettered by John Costanza, and Watchmen, lettered by Dave Gibbons, in his office. He drew a face from that tradition: hand-lettered, informal, cheerfully irregular. It is not an imitation of either, but it comes from the same place.

Then he finished it too late, and it never shipped in Bob at all. It went out with 3D Movie Maker instead, another product with cartoon guides and speech bubbles, and from there into Windows — onto tens of millions of desktops, sitting in the font menu next to Arial and Times New Roman.

That is the whole story of the hatred, and it has nothing to do with the drawing. For roughly a decade, Comic Sans was the only informal typeface most people owned. Anyone making a birthday flyer, a lost-cat poster, a church newsletter — anyone who wanted to sound like a human rather than a memo — had exactly one lever, and pulled it. Including, inevitably, people announcing funerals and delivering test results.

Blaming the typeface for that is like blaming a hammer for a room full of things that turned out not to be nails. The design brief was cartoon speech bubbles. It performs that brief well. It was simply the only tool in the drawer.

## Papyrus is a twenty-three-year-old's sincere idea

Chris Costello drew Papyrus in 1982, aged twenty-three and just out of college. He had been reading the Bible, and started wondering what writing would have looked like in the Middle East at that time — rough surface, reed pen, irregular edges. He hand-drew the whole thing over about six months with a calligraphy pen on textured paper. Letraset released it in 1983.

Read that again as a piece of work rather than a punchline. Six months of hand-drawing, from a coherent idea, by someone barely out of school. Most typefaces are worse than Papyrus and almost none of them are as clear about what they are trying to be.

What happened next is the same thing that happened to Comic Sans: it shipped with everything, it became the only vaguely ancient or organic option most people had, and it went onto every yoga studio, herbal tea box and Mediterranean restaurant menu in the world. Then it went onto a blockbuster film's subtitles, and became a joke with a much larger audience.

Costello has been remarkably gracious about all of it, which is more than most of us would manage.

## So what is actually wrong with them?

Nothing, in the drawing. The problem is ubiquity plus a narrow brief.

A typeface designed for one specific tone, distributed to everyone, will be used for every tone. The face itself carries a strong voice — that is what it was hired for — and when the voice does not match the message, the mismatch is loud and it is the typeface you can see. Nobody looks at a funeral notice in Comic Sans and thinks poor tool selection by the bereaved. They think that font is awful.

The tell is that neither face is criticised on typographic grounds. Nobody says Papyrus has bad spacing, or that Comic Sans has a weak italic. The complaint is always about where it turned up. That is a criticism of a decision, not a drawing.

## The genuinely bad ones

Here is what actually makes a typeface bad, and none of it is fun to argue about:

- Characters you cannot tell apart. A capital I, a lowercase l and a numeral 1 drawn as the same vertical bar. An O and a zero with no distinguishing mark. This is the failure that costs someone a wrong digit in a serial number, and it is the one thing where the typeface genuinely outranks the setting.

- Spacing that was never done. Plenty of free fonts are a nice set of drawings with no kerning and default sidebearings. They look fine as a word in a specimen and fall apart as a paragraph, with holes after every capital and collisions on every AV pair.

- A character set that stops at the edge of English. No accents, so the moment someone writes café or Zoë the browser silently swaps in a different font mid-word.

- Weights that are not related. A "family" where the bold is just the regular with a stroke added, so the counters close up and the proportions shift. You notice it instantly and cannot say why.

- Hinting that gives up on Windows. A face that is beautiful on a Mac and a smear on a ClearType screen at 13px. Half the world is on the other machine.

These are the real failures, and they are almost never the fonts on the lists — because a font has to be popular to be hated, and popularity usually means somebody did the boring work.

## The campaign, and its ending

Ban Comic Sans was started by Dave and Holly Combs, graphic designers in Indianapolis, after an employer insisted they use the font for a children's museum exhibit — which, in fairness, is close to the one context it was built for. It became a manifesto, stickers, a genuine internet movement.

A note on sourcing: reference works disagree on the year it began, giving both 1999 and 2002. I have left the date out rather than pick one.

The part worth knowing is how it ended. The Combses wound the campaign down in 2019, with Dave Combs saying the hatred had got out of hand. The joke had stopped being a joke about typography and had turned into a way of sneering at people who had never been taught to choose a typeface and had no reason to know.

> The campaign against the world’s most hated font was ended by the people who started it, because the hating got mean.

## The uncomfortable footnote

Comic Sans is widely used in schools, and it has two properties that legibility research actually supports: characters that resist being confused with their own mirror images, and unusually wide spacing. Those are real virtues, and they are the same mechanism that makes a licence plate readable.

That is not a claim that it is a remedy. No typeface is — the research on faces sold for dyslexia has repeatedly failed to find a measurable benefit. But it does mean the most mocked typeface of the last thirty years is doing something defensible for the readers who use it most, and the people mocking it mostly have not checked.

## What a type designer takes from this

Two things, and the first stings.

If you draw a face with a strong voice and give it away to everyone, you are signing up for it to be used badly, publicly, forever. That is not a reason to draw bland type. It is a reason to be clear-eyed that reach and control are traded against each other, and that the trade is permanent.

The second is about where criticism should point. Choosing type badly is a skill problem, and skill problems are fixable with a sentence of advice. Ridiculing the tool teaches nobody anything and mostly signals membership. If a menu is set in Papyrus, the useful response is that the face is doing all the talking and the words cannot get a word in — not that the owner is an idiot.

Vigil is a quiet face on purpose, which is a different bet: less voice, more range, harder to use conspicuously wrong. That is not virtue. It is just a different trade, and it comes with its own failure mode — nobody ever loved a typeface for being sensible.
